data.title: Severn Trent under fire for boasting it hasn’t banned hosepipes
data.description:
Severn Trent has come under fire because of claims it is sending the “wrong message” by telling customers it has not enforced a hosepipe ban for more than three decades.

At a meeting with the Environment Agency, the government watchdog, officials criticised a notice on the water utility’s website about its record on hosepipe bans at a time when customers are being told to save water.

The company’s website proclaims: “Right now, there is no hosepipe ban in place for Severn Trent customers. We’ve not had one in our area since 1995, and of course we’d like that to continue.”

The way the claim was communicated came in for criticism at a meeting in July, according to notes seen by The Times.

One official “noted we are still using the ‘we haven’t had a hosepipe ban in 30 years’ and feels it sends the wrong message”, according to the document.

Severn Trent staff said the message was included on its website to reassure customers who mistakenly believed a ban was in place and to encourage them “to do their part to continue not having restrictions”.

Hosepipe bans are in force across swathes of southern England and the Midlands as well as south-western Wales, affecting more than 27 million people.

However, Severn Trent’s nine million customers are not covered by water use restrictions.

Public communications are considered a critical part of encouraging people to reduce water use in times of drought.

Severn Trent’s public drought plan includes details of the communications it uses at different stages of water shortages.

These begin with marketing campaigns to promote the use of water butts and save-a-flush devices. If restrictions are to be introduced, the plan moves on to paid advertising to encourage consumers and companies to cut back on water use.

During a hosepipe ban, the company has a plan for “intense local broadcast activity” across “all traditional media (TV/radio/newspapers) as well as social media”. Its adverts will deliver “hard messaging” to drive home the importance of cutting water use.

Severn Trent said it has no plan to remove the current message from its website despite criticism from officials. A spokesman said: “We actively engage and work collaboratively with the EA on drought planning so that we can do the right thing for our customers and the environment. Our focus is on working around the clock, treating more water and fixing leaks at record levels.”

An Environment Agency spokesman said: “We all have a role to play in using a little less water to make sure our current water reserves last. Every drop we can save is a drop more for our farmers, wildlife and rivers.

“We expect water companies to follow their drought plans to ensure supplies are not disrupted in even the driest of weather.”

data.title: The foreign suppliers propping up a ‘Made in Britain’ defence boom
data.description:
As prototypes of the Challenger 3 battle tank arrived at a factory in Shropshire two years ago, they were hailed by the then-Conservative government as the first “fully British” tank built in more than 20 years.

It was an eye-catching claim and there’s certainly no doubt the £1.3bn upgrade programme for the Army’s armoured vehicles is bringing jobs and investment to the economy.

But is it true? The answer, strictly speaking, is no.

Though the Challenger 3 tanks are mostly British – using domestically-made armour, turrets and gun sights – they are being produced by a German-controlled company, make use of a German-made main gun and are equipped with Israeli-made active protection systems.

The reason for this is prosaic rather than nefarious, says Francis Tusa, an independent defence analyst.

“If you wanted to get anything within five years, the UK didn’t actually have the industrial capacity and capability to do these things,” he explains.

It highlights a major conundrum – and political risk – for the Government as Labour launches a fresh drive to “back British”.

With military spending on the rise once again, ministers have pledged to ensure that more of this money is funnelled towards the UK economy instead of overseas.

This includes a promise, outlined in June’s defence investment plan, to “weight procurement decisions towards British companies that can demonstrate a genuine, substantive presence and long-term commitment to British communities and British supply chains.”

As part of this, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) has said it will define what a “British company” is and use it to enforce a “buy British by default” rule.

The initiative also aims to give the UK more control over its own equipment, including what it can supply to Ukraine, amid concerns that export controls on kit made by the US and some European allies have left the military too constrained.

But though the moves have been broadly welcomed, industry sources say Labour’s patriotic push is also prompting a new phenomenon: “Britwashing”.

‘Slap a British flag on’

Similar to so-called greenwashing, where companies make tokenistic gestures to embellish their eco-credentials, this is where companies exaggerate their Britishness to improve their chances of securing lucrative government contracts.

And as lobbyists ramp up their campaigns to build a variety of unmanned aircraft, troop vehicles and naval vessels for the MoD, some are sailing fairly close to the wind.

“It’s pretty widespread,” says a source at a major defence company, who points to adverts designed to catch the eyes of MPs as they pass through Westminster’s Underground station.

“There are some firms that think all they need to do is just slap a British flag on their stuff or put ‘UK’ at the end of their name.”

In the past, says Tusa, this might best have been applied to equipment supplied by American defence contractors, where small numbers of jobs created in the UK for the supply of minor components were touted as domestic wins.

“It’s hiding the fact that it comes from an American factory, all the jobs are in America and all the intellectual property is American,” he adds.

“Traditionally, it was all a bit ‘nudge nudge, wink wink’.

“If you had challenged people at the MoD and even the Treasury and said, ‘That’s not British, is it?’, they’d have probably given a Hugh Grant-esque ruffling of their hair, a shrugging of the shoulders, a bit of a grin and said, ‘Well, that’s the game, isn’t it?’”

But with Donald Trump’s capricious style of foreign policy unnerving European capitals, many countries including Britain are seeking to hedge their bets by moving production back home or working more closely with allies on the Continent.

Tusa adds: “We’re on the cusp of something at the moment.

“If they are serious, we are going to have to see people really challenging the statements on jobs.

“You can’t have just a brass nameplate ‘British’ company with a solicitor’s office and £100 of assets.”

Yet it’s also valid to question what ministers really mean when they say “British” – particularly as the domestic defence industry has been reliant on American and European suppliers for decades.

Take production of the Royal Air Force’s Eurofighter Typhoon jets – a multinational collaboration in which Britain secured a 37pc share of the work needed to produce the jet.

Or the Army’s new AW149 medium helicopters. These are described as a “sovereign” capability but Leonardo’s factory in Yeovil, Somerset, will do only 40pc of the work (rising to as much as 70pc when lifetime maintenance and upgrades are included).

That is significantly higher than the 5pc that the UK received from the latest order of Apache helicopters it secured from American giant Boeing, or the 3pc to 6pc work share for the manufacture of Chinooks for the RAF.

But there are often good reasons for not doing everything domestically – not least on price and capability grounds.

Take ships for example.

BAE and Babcock are building the Royal Navy’s Type 26 and Type 31 frigates, respectively, with largely foreign-supplied steel.

A spokesman for BAE says the company tries to use British steel “wherever possible”, but points out that domestic suppliers often don’t produce the specialist categories needed for military purposes.

It is also difficult to persuade steelmakers to start new production lines because the low volumes needed for defence projects are – in the context of the wider steel industry – trivial and not worth the investment.

Another example where the lack of domestic options is becoming apparent is the Army’s competition to replace its long-serving fleet of Land Rovers.

Battling for contracts

Some of the world’s biggest motoring and defence giants are vying to provide a successor, but almost none of them are based on vehicles made in Britain.

Babcock, the domestic defence giant, has proposed a “best of British” vehicle based on the Toyota Land Cruiser, while British billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Automotive has offered a militarised version of its Grenadier Quartermaster – the base of which will be made in France (Ineos says it will be 70pc British overall).

Other contenders include General Motors and General Dynamics, which are respectively proposing versions of Chevrolet and Ford pickup trucks made in the US.

German giant Rheinmetall has also put forward a vehicle adapted from the Mercedes-Benz G-Class.

Even Jaguar Land Rover, if it decided to compete, might have questions to answer. The modern version of the Land Rover Defender is currently made in Slovakia.

Only Fering, a UK start-up which is proposing the military-grade Pioneer X, is claiming to have an all-British design and is proposing to manufacture the cars in Battersea, south London.

The Army’s initial order will be for 3,000 vehicles and will be worth around £900m, with a victor yet to be decided.

It’s just one example of several high-profile procurement decisions that will test the MoD’s commitment to Britishness.

Another is the £360m competition to replace the RAF’s ageing fleet of Hawk training jets – including those used by the Red Arrows – by 2030.

Contenders include an American-Swedish model made by Boeing and Saab, an Italian jet by Leonardo, one from Korea Aerospace Industries and US giant Lockheed Martin and another by Turkish Aerospace Industries.

Both the Boeing-Saab jet and Leonardo’s offering could be assembled in the UK.

A British contender had been put forward by start-up Aeralis, but the company collapsed into administration earlier this year.

Still, buying the domestic choice is not always the right answer.

Overseas capabilities

Defence industry executives often point out that different countries have come to specialise in certain areas over the years – and that if Nato allies work together, they can augment each other’s strengths rather than compete.

German giant Renk is the biggest supplier of tank gearboxes globally, for example, because it is exceptionally good at making them. Likewise, Leonardo is the global leader in laser targeting and guidance systems – which it makes at its electronics base in Edinburgh.

Not everyone wants to specialise, however. France is perhaps the pre-eminent example of a country that has taken the opposite approach, partly out of a belief that Europe should not rely on America.

Paris has long insisted on retaining its own sovereign capabilities across the military spectrum, from its nuclear deterrent to the Rafale fighter jet and Leclerc battle tank.

It’s this impulse that prompted French aerospace giant Dassault and the German arm of Airbus to part ways because of a next-generation fighter jet.

In this sense, many industry insiders argue Britain’s lack of certain industrial capabilities was not inevitable either.

In private, many blame gaps that have opened up since the end of the Cold War on a persistent push by the Treasury to save money.

Across successive decades, as politicians have sought to divert money to other priorities such as healthcare and benefits, the MoD has often been pressured to forgo more expensive, domestically produced kit in favour of ostensibly cheaper, “off-the-shelf” alternatives made abroad.

Ironically, says Tusa, this was the reason why German giant Rheinmetall had to be brought in to help restore production of gun barrels for the Challenger 3 tank.

“That was a capability BAE Systems previously had – they were doing it for M777 artillery pieces – but years ago, they said to the Government, ‘We’ve got this barrel-forging plant, do you still want this capability onshore?’ and the numpties at the MoD said they weren’t interested.”

Now that money is flowing back into the defence budget, however, there is pressure to restore some of what has been lost and ensure ministers can point to tangible benefits for British workers.

For example, Rheinmetall has invested more than £40m in its Telford, Shropshire, site, including in a gun hall that will restore Britain’s capability to produce 120mm and 155mm barrels and breeches.

The German company has hailed the programme as a “powerful example of how Britain can work with trusted allies without compromising its own industrial base”.

In doing so, it has pointed to work being done by domestic firms, including Newcastle-based turret maker Pearson Engineering, seating manufacturer NP Aerospace in the West Midlands and power-management provider Atec Engineering Solutions in Manchester.

It will not only deliver 148 upgraded tanks for the Army, a spokesman says, but also rebuild the “skills, facilities, supply chains, intellectual property and industrial capacity” Britain needs to make armoured vehicles “for decades to come”.

Elsewhere, rearmament is spawning entirely new businesses who have made their Britishness a key selling point.

One is Cambridge Aerospace, which was recently valued at $3.4bn (£2.5bn) because of the low-cost drone and missile interceptors it has developed.

The company has secured contracts with the MoD and been praised by ministers as a “prime case of a veteran-founded UK defence start-up”.

Another one of the companies tapping into increased demand for defence and aerospace components is London-based Isembard.

The start-up – founded by Alex Fitzgerald, an Army reservist and former broadband entrepreneur – is building a distributed network of factories that can churn out machined metal parts quickly and cheaply.

“Our customers tell us that we’re actually cheaper and faster than our Chinese rivals when it comes to complex parts,” Fitzgerald says.

He started his business after becoming convinced that Britain and its allies needed to modernise their defence industries rapidly to help deter the likes of Russia and China.

“A country’s ability to defend itself is a function of its will and capability,” he says. “And capability is not just the equipment you have at the start but what you learn you need as any conflict takes place.

“Everyone’s obsessed about the product layer, but no one’s thinking enough about the industrial layer – whether it’s a drone, a missile, a submarine or a satellite, these things are all made of parts.”

‘A hell of a lot of effort’

Fitzgerald supports efforts to capture more value for the UK and believes ministers should consider a domestic version of the strict US international traffic in arms regulations to ensure manufacturing of home-grown designs stays onshore.

He also believes “made in the UK” should mean just that, including most of the manufactured components: “And if you’re not doing that, then it’s bull---t.”

With requirements for Britishness seemingly becoming stricter, drone producers such as Anglo-Portuguese Tekever and US-based Anduril are also stepping up their UK operations.

Ultimately, however, the lengths companies will go to depend on how hard the Government pushes for British-made goods and whether it is worth it.

“Is it possible to build every single defence capability we want in the UK, from everything down to bolts?” asks Tusa.

“Yeah, absolutely. Will it take an awful lot of time? Also yes.

“It’s like pushing a broken-down car. To get the bloody thing moving, it takes a hell of a lot of effort – but once you’ve got it rolling, less so.”

An MoD spokesman said: “We are committed to backing British businesses and supporting our defence industrial and skills base, making defence an engine for growth in every postcode across the UK.”

data.title: TikTok investigates potential UK sanctions breach
data.description:
TikTok is investigating a possible breach of UK sanctions after flagging concerns to a Treasury watchdog.

The Chinese-owned video-sharing business said on Thursday that it had reported itself to the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) because of a “potential issue” linked to sanctions rules.

TikTok, which is owned by China-headquartered ByteDance, refused to disclose what the possible breach may have involved.

The Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) is an arm of the Treasury, which enforces sanctions rules.

Its sanctions list covers hundreds of individuals worldwide, as well as dozens of Russian businesses, front companies and energy giants.

The disclosure by TikTok’s international arm, which includes the UK and most major markets outside the US and China, comes after the social media business was forced to carve off its American division under threats from Donald Trump.

According to accounts for the international arm, TikTok Information Technologies UK, the business also set aside $1.05bn for potential legal battles and regulatory investigations. This was 13pc higher than last year.

TikTok was split in two in January, with its US business transferred to a new company, USDS Joint Venture, partly owned by US investors, while Beijing-headquartered ByteDance kept a minority shareholding.

The social media company, known for its viral videos, has faced years of scrutiny because of its ownership and China’s influence on the business. TikTok always denied posing a national security risk.

After facing an outright block in the US, Mr Trump delayed the ban until a deal was agreed to spin off its US app.

TikTok has previously faced hundreds of millions in fines from European watchdogs and a series of investigations because of issues such as data processing and child safety.

Ofcom, Britain’s communications watchdog, began a formal investigation last month into whether it is protecting children from being exposed to harmful material online.

TikTok said at the time that it “strictly enforces age-appropriate experiences” and that it had invested billions in child safety.

According to accounts filed with Companies House this week, TikTok’s international revenues climbed to $9.2bn (£6.74bn), up 45.7pc. It also swung to a profit of almost $452m.

The business represents TikTok’s operations across the UK, Europe, South and Central America and Africa. In China, a separate app, Douyin, acts as a sister business to TikTok.

The OFSI, the UK’s sanctions regulator, has been cracking down on companies caught doing business with Russia, with some £28.7bn of frozen Russian assets reported to the regulator.

It handed Apple a £390,000 penalty in March for two payments that the tech giant accidentally made to a Russian streaming app in 2022.

The watchdog said Apple was not aware that the app was owned by a bank controlled by Moscow that was sanctioned when it made the payments.

TikTok and OFSI declined to comment.

data.title: Labour’s Left is scrambling to save net zero. Burnham should ignore them
data.description:
If any doubt remained about the ineffectiveness of Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills, the latest price cap figures surely put an end to any such debate.

The Prime Minister’s pledge, which came just days after his inauguration, was an attempt to show that the Government under his new leadership was serious about helping struggling households tackle the cost of living.

The temporary tax break was intended to save households an average of £45 a year and “give families some breathing room on bills and provide some reassurance this winter”, John Healey, the Chancellor, said at the time.

Yet the savings from Burnham’s great energy giveaway are set to be completely wiped out by a 4pc average increase – equivalent to £66 for a typical household – in household bills this October, according to energy research group Cornwall Insight.

As for Labour’s manifesto pledge to bring down energy bills by £300, that is “in tatters”, Richard Tice, Reform UK’s energy spokesman, claimed – not unreasonably.

Against this damning backdrop, some Labour figures – mostly on the Left of the party – are desperately scrambling to salvage an energy policy with net zero at its very heart. This is despite a mounting wall of evidence that such a commitment is built on a false promise of cheaper energy.

The latest rearguard action came in response to analysis showing the Government’s full-throttle dash to build a so-called “clean” electricity grid is achieving the exact opposite of what it claims.

Rather than delivering affordable energy that makes us all wealthier, the research – conducted by Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy secretary, and centre-Right think tank Onward – shows the complete opposite: Britain is in fact becoming “poorer and weaker”, as Coutinho puts it.

The shadow energy secretary and Onward offer a genuinely credible alternative in which electricity would be nearly 80pc clean by using “a bit more gas and a lot more nuclear”, in her words. It would also be, crucially, “much cheaper”.

Predictably, the study sent some of Labour’s net zero acolytes into meltdown.

Jeevun Sandher, a key aide to Coutinho’s opposite number Miatta Fahnbulleh, claimed on X that it didn’t add up because the “modelling assumes natural gas prices are low and stable over the next 25 years, gradually falling over time”.

Yet there have been “two gas price shocks in four years, caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz”, he said.

Coutinho’s riposte to Sandher’s perceived “gotcha” was swift and brutal.

“It’s your own department’s central forecast,” she pointed out before delivering the mother of all put-downs: “These people are absolute clowns.”

Harsh, perhaps, but not unjustified. Labour’s energy policy has long resembled a circus with Ed Miliband in the starring role of manipulative, evil ringmaster.

Replacing him with Fahnbulleh offers a modicum of reassurance after she suggested the 2050 net zero timetable could be slowed, in contrast to her predecessor, who departed with a call for Labour’s climate actions to be “faster, deeper and more wide-ranging”.

What has the Left’s net zero zealots truly in a tizz is the fear that Burnham is more inclined to prioritise the cost of living and economic growth instead of arbitrary clean power deadlines after he removed net zero requirements from public procurement.

The Prime Minister is also expected to approve North Sea drilling after promising to adopt a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas exploration.

Sandher’s intervention is a reminder of the resistance among some influential Labour figures that net zero opponents are up against.

The Prime Minister should ignore the endless catastrophising of the “climate emergency” brigade that Sandher appears to be a fully-fledged member of.

He should instead focus on the facts, or what Coutinho calls the “hidden costs of relying on wind and solar”.

They are, after all, plentiful: paying for back-up power when the wind stops blowing, subsidising wind farms that have to turn off when it’s too windy and the grid can’t cope, and the cost of erecting several thousand more pylons to transmit the electricity from offshore wind farms in Scotland to the south where it’s most needed.

As Onward points out, Burnham’s VAT cut is merely a continuation of a long-established approach that treats the symptoms not the cause and shifts costs between different groups.

The £150 annual warm homes discount for poorer households, for example, is funded by a £40 levy on household bills.

Yet none of these schemes fix the problem, which is that the UK is having to build an expensive underlying system to enable it to shift to net zero under an entirely self-imposed timeline.

The outcome of this is that Britain is blighted by the highest electricity prices in the developed world and rather than bills coming down by £300, as Labour promised, they’ve gone up by £300 instead.

What’s more, many experts expect them to rise even further in the next four years because of network upgrade costs and subsidies.

With the case against net zero rapidly mounting, the Left is trying to scare Burnham into believing that abandoning the target would be politically ruinous.

A recent poll shows support for green policies is waning, yet Sandher has urged the Government to ignore the findings on the basis they are “driven by falls in support by hardcore Reform and Conservative voters who do not support us and never will”.

Labour voters, meanwhile, “see our planet burning and our voters get the need to deal with it”, he said.

While it’s true that support for net zero has dropped more steeply on the Right, what Sandher is less forthcoming about is that it is falling among Labour voters too – just not as sharply.

What is even more disingenuous is the suggestion that anyone who rejects net zero isn’t serious about tackling climate change. As Coutinho points out, it is possible to have cleaner electricity that is also cheaper.

But it would mean accepting the need for a small and temporary increase in gas, and much more nuclear, rather than doubling down on intermittent wind and solar.

Burnham should ignore the fearmongering. Presented with a more proportionate and pragmatic alternative that leaves them better, not considerably poorer, I suspect most clear-minded voters would bite his hand off.

data.title: Richard Branson’s Virgin to take on Eurostar with 20 trains a day
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson’s ambition to run trains between London and Paris has taken a critical step forward after Virgin won permission to use the route to the Channel Tunnel.

The British billionaire’s company is bidding to launch a rival service to Eurostar by 2030 and will need to use the tracks between St Pancras International in north London and the tunnel entrance in Folkestone, Kent.

It has now won approval from regulators at the Office for Rail and Road (ORR) to do just that. The ORR has signed off on an earlier agreement struck with HS1 Limited, also known as London St Pancras High Speed.

A separate agreement will be needed for Virgin Trains to use the tunnel itself, which is owned by Paris-based Getlink, as well as further regulatory approvals.

However, a Virgin Group spokesman said its plans were “moving at pace” and it was on track to meet its 2030 launch date.

Sir Richard’s company hopes to run up to 20 trains a day in competition with Eurostar, the sole operator of services currently.

The services would ultimately run between London and Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam.

Martin Jones, of the ORR, said: “This is an important next step in bringing competition and growth to the market for international rail services, and we welcome the progress Virgin Trains and London St Pancras High Speed have made.

“While there is still more work to do, we are supporting Virgin and the wider industry to grow international services.”

A Virgin Group spokesman added: “We welcome the ORR’s pre-approval of our track access agreement and the opportunity to bring competition and Virgin’s award-winning customer experience to the Channel Tunnel.”

Virgin Trains is one of several rail companies vying to challenge Eurostar’s long-standing dominance of the London-to-Paris route.

Trenitalia, Gemini Trains and Evolyn are also seeking access to the Channel Tunnel.

Critics have argued that a lack of competition currently gives too much pricing power to Eurostar’s passenger services, which were found to charge “nearly twice the European average per kilometre” by campaign group Transport & Environment in 2024.

Upon launch, Virgin hopes to run 13 return trains a day to Paris, against Eurostar’s 14 services. Sir Richard’s company hopes to run four a day from London to Brussels, compared with eight or nine services operated by Eurostar each day; and three to Amsterdam, against Eurostar’s five.

Under European rail rules, it has been possible for rivals to apply to use the route for more than a decade but strict safety regulations previously meant trains had to be specially adapted for the tunnel.

Deutsche Bahn obtained permission to use the Channel Tunnel in 2013 but later abandoned its plans after struggling to get approval for its trains in Belgium.

In 2023, the restrictions on the tunnel were eased to allow less-specialised trains to be used – clearing the way for more competition.

For Virgin, another obstacle was cleared last year when it was authorised to use spare capacity at Temple Mills, the only high-speed train depot on the British side, in Leyton, east London.

Trenitalia is separately building a new depot on the French side, just outside Paris.

A Eurostar spokesman said of the ORR decision: “This confirms the huge potential for growth in international rail and the ambition across the industry to bring more passengers to Europe by train.

“Eurostar will play a full part in that growth, and our focus remains on delivering our own ambitious plans, investing in our fleet and carrying 30 million passengers a year.”

Getlink was approached for comment.

data.title: Mike Ashley tightens grip on Hugo Boss after takeover bid
data.description:
Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group has built an almost 50pc stake in Hugo Boss after failing to take control of the German fashion brand.

The retailer now owns 48pc of Hugo Boss after shareholders agreed to sell a further 17.6pc of the company to Mr Ashley’s retail empire.

It comes after Frasers made an offer in June for the remaining shares in the German brand that it did not already own. The bid of €38 (£32.50) per share valued the business at €2.7bn.

That approach was rejected by Hugo Boss’s board, who said the offer undervalued the business and its prospects, but Frasers said on Tuesday it had been accepted by a minority of shareholders.

The result leaves Mr Ashley’s retail business just short of outright control, but with a major influence over the future of one of Europe’s best-known fashion groups.

Frasers began building its stake in Hugo Boss in 2020 and crossed the 30pc threshold earlier this year, triggering a mandatory offer for the remaining business under German market rules.

Michael Murray, Frasers’ chief executive and Mr Ashley’s son-in-law, is also a member of the Hugo Boss supervisory board. He did not take part in discussions about Frasers’ takeover offer because of the potential conflict of interest.

Hugo Boss generated €4.3bn in sales last year and is in the midst of a turnaround drive after a slowdown in the luxury fashion market.

Frasers’ pursuit of Hugo Boss comes as the Sports Direct owner expands its push into high-end retail.

It already owns shares in Mulberry and Burberry, upping its stake in the latter to 4.16pc in July. The company’s Flannels chain has become one of Britain’s biggest fashion retailers.

The FTSE 100 retailer also bought Harvey Nichols in a pre-pack administration deal last week for a reported £40m, taking control of the department store’s UK business and more than 1,000 employees.

It has previously described its plans for luxury shopping as a natural progression after building its business on discount retailer Sports Direct.

The Hugo Boss deal leaves Frasers as the company’s biggest shareholder by a wide margin. It could continue buying shares in future, although the group has not indicated whether it intends to make another attempt to take full control.

Frasers has previously said the offer had been an opportunity to create “a stronger, more resilient and more successful” Hugo Boss. Mr Ashley vowed in a recent interview with the Financial Times to “show them a bit of Dunkirk spirit”.

data.title: Water companies to charge more during droughts
data.description:
Water companies will be able to charge consumers higher prices during droughts under plans being considered by Ofwat.

Firms will be allowed to impose “surge pricing” and factor “water scarcity” into bills as part of a drive to reduce consumption.

This would clear the way for suppliers to introduce prices that change based on the time of year and escalate if consumers pass a certain threshold.

Most of the new pricing schemes would require households to have smart meters.

Details about the plans have emerged just days after three quarters of the country was declared in drought, with 27 million people living under hosepipe bans, while wildfires have been raging in large parts of the UK.

The proposals would take effect from April, if they were given final approval by regulator Ofwat in the coming weeks.

Angela Eagle, the Environment Secretary, previously described regulation of the water sector as “toothless” and pledged “fundamental reform”.

Feargal Sharkey, the water campaigner and former Undertones singer, said suppliers were “once again” penalising consumers for their own failures.

“For 40 years, these companies have had legal obligations to help consumers to reduce their demand and they have failed at that comprehensively, just as they’ve failed to keep our rivers clean and failed to deal with our sewage,” he said.

“Now they’re going to penalise consumers for that failure.”

There are different ways suppliers could use the new powers.

Under seasonal surge pricing customers could be charged more during the summer and less in winter, while rising block tariffs would charge higher prices when consumers pass a certain threshold of water use.

Surge pricing would create an incentive for households to save water at a time when experts are increasingly worried by the droughts affecting Britain.

The changes have been backed in principle by both Labour and the water industry, but could prove controversial at a time when utility companies are already under fire for raising bills.

There are no formal plans by companies to introduce widespread surge pricing yet, but Ofwat’s consultation said suppliers regarded the current rules as a block on doing so.

On Thursday, five suppliers – Severn Trent, Southern Water, Thames Water, Wessex Water and South East Water – were granted permission by Ofwat to raise bills above previously agreed levels to support higher spending on improving infrastructure.

In response, Andy Burnham accused water companies of treating consumers like “a blank cheque”.

Commenting on the surge pricing proposals, Mr Sharkey added: “We’ve all been treated with contempt and forced to pay for our own exploitation for decades. Ofwat is once again doing nothing to rein in an industry that is clearly out of control.”

However, Water UK, which represents suppliers, said that, as well as tackling leaks, the industry needed to look at “rewarding people through their water bill”.

The proposals to formalise surge pricing follow small trials in several parts of the country, the largest covering about 14,000 Anglian Water households in Lincoln and Norwich.

Customers have seen their water costs increase from £2.69 per cubic metre to as much as £4.39 from May to August. For the rest of the year, it is reduced to £1.78 per cubic metre. Vulnerable and poorer customers are excluded from the scheme.

Around half of customers cut their consumption in response. Anglian Water is considering expanding the scheme.

Seasonal and block-pricing have also been trialled by South West Water.

Under block pricing, those using “essential” amounts of water pay a basic rate, with usage levels such as “standard” and “premium” carrying higher costs.

This would penalise households who use hoses or sprinklers to water their gardens.

Ministers want to cut the average consumption of water per person per day from about 136.5 litres today to 122 litres by 2038.

An Ofwat spokesman said: “The efficient use of water is in the best interests of everyone, including businesses.

“The options we are progressing would support greater consideration of water scarcity and efficiency by water companies when setting their charges.”

A government spokesman said: “This Government is committed to championing consumers and protecting households from cost of living pressures.

“We have already ring-fenced money earmarked for new infrastructure so it can only be spent on fixing the problems, and will go further by fundamentally reforming the water sector so that it works for the public, keeping bills as low as they can be.

“Water companies are trialling new charging structures which must, as promised, make bills fairer and more affordable while encouraging greater water efficiency.”

data.title: Disabled people to get free bus travel 24 hours a day
data.description:
Disabled people in England will be able to travel on buses for free at all hours of the day from next year.

Restrictions on disabled bus passes will be lifted in April under plans to tackle the cost of living.

The passes are currently valid for travel only on weekdays from 9.30am to 11pm unless local authorities fund an extension, as Greater Manchester did earlier this year under Andy Burnham, the former mayor.

Plans to remove the time restriction will cost £60m and the funds will come from existing budgets – with £40m from the Department for Work and Pensions and £20m from the Department for Transport.

Since entering No 10, Mr Burnham has announced several policies aimed at tackling the rising cost of living, including cutting business rates for pubs, capping bus fares at £2 and scrapping VAT on electricity bills.

On Monday, the Prime Minister said: “Buses are a lifeline for so many people – making it easier to get to work, education and healthcare.

“It’s simply not right that many disabled people cannot travel using their pass during certain times of the day. So we’re fixing that. Disabled people will now have unlimited free bus travel 24/7.

“I did it before in Greater Manchester and I’m proud to do it now for the whole country. This is part of our ongoing action to bring back hope and give people some much-needed breathing space on the cost of living.”

‘This is a huge win’

James Taylor, an executive director at Scope, the disability charity, said the move would “remove barriers to everyday life” for disabled people.

Tom Gordon, a Liberal Democrat MP who had been campaigning for the change for almost two years, said: “Disabilities don’t start at 9am – neither should disabled bus passes and soon enough they won’t.” He added: “This is a huge win for the disabled community.”

The MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough had been looking to force a second Commons vote seeking to remove the time restrictions this September after MPs rejected his first attempt last year.

A Conservative Party spokesman said: “This is simply the shuffling around of existing departmental budgets. Andy Burnham needs to come clean about how he is going to fund this growing list of policies.”

The Government introduced free bus travel for under-16s in August, though the scheme is optional for bus companies.

data.title: M&S named fastest-growing grocer in Britain
data.description:
Marks & Spencer has been named Britain’s fastest-growing grocer after sales surged during the summer heatwave.

Food sales at M&S jumped 15.9pc in the 12 weeks to Aug 10 compared with the previous year, comfortably ahead of its rivals, according to retail analysts Worldpanel by Numerator.

Sales growth accelerated as the heatwave took hold. Grocery spending rose 11.7pc in the 12 weeks to June, before climbing 16pc in the following 12 weeks – its fastest growth rate since May 2023.

M&S has spent £30m cutting prices on more than 65 everyday products this year as it tries to make its food halls more competitive.

It has dropped the price of fresh salmon fillets, with two Caledonian Gold fillets falling from £5.50 to £4.95, and made further cuts to staples such as minced beef, free-range eggs and tomato ketchup.

British supermarkets were also boosted by booming sales of chilled finger foods, as shoppers basked in record-breaking temperatures.

Sales of cold dips climbed 23pc while finger foods climbed 15.2pc, quiche sales were up 15.8pc and olive sales rose by 13.3pc.

M&S has billed itself as the “undisputed home of picky bits”.

M&S’s summer growth rate was well ahead of rival supermarkets and grocers, Worldpanel found. Only Ocado, the online grocery business, came close, with sales increasing by 13.1pc.

Tesco’s sales rose 1.8pc, while Sainsbury’s grew 3.5pc and Morrisons was up 3.3pc. Aldi increased sales by 1.1pc and Lidl surged 8.5pc.

Asda was the only major supermarket to suffer a fall, with sales down 0.2pc.

The struggling grocer has now gone without sales growth since March 2024, despite a push by Allan Leighton, the executive chairman, to win back customers with lower prices.

The latest figures still were an improvement on the previous period, when Asda’s sales fell 1.1pc. Its market share also edged up to 11.9pc from 11.5pc a year earlier.

But Asda remains well behind Tesco and Sainsbury’s, which account for 27.8pc and 15.1pc of grocery spending respectively. It is only narrowly ahead of Aldi, which has 10.9pc. Worldpanel does not break out M&S’s grocery market share.

Asda plunged to a loss of almost £1bn last year after sales fell 3.4pc, while its debt interest bill climbed to £730m.

It has responded with aggressive price cuts, but Mr Leighton has warned that the strategy would come at a “material” cost to profits.

An Asda spokesman said: “The latest figures show continued improvement with sales down just 0.2pc – an improvement of 0.9pc on the previous period. As Worldpanel notes, this represents our best performance since March 2024.”

data.title: Currys’ turnaround king tasked with reviving tired Boots ahead of flotation
data.description:
When Currys announced that Alex Baldock, its chief executive, was stepping down earlier this year, the response from investors was immediate.

Shares in the electronics chain fell sharply – wiping almost 11pc off its valuation – as markets digested the departure of the man widely credited with engineering the company’s quietly successful turnaround.

Now Baldock appears poised for an even bigger challenge, tasked with reviving a 177-year-old brand that has seen better days. On Wednesday, it emerged that the outgoing Currys chief was being lined up to take the reins at Boots.

The company confirmed his appointment on Thursday, setting the stage for Baldock to try to convince investors that the British chemist could be worth as much as £7bn.

Baldock should be well-suited to the role. He has spent the past seven years proving that legacy retailers can still thrive if they modernise quickly enough.

At Currys, that meant slimming down the store estate, cutting costs, boosting online sales and emphasising its “omnichannel” offering of services, repairs, credit and subscriptions.

Adam Tomlinson, a retail analyst at Berenberg, says that when Baldock arrived at Currys in 2018, “the business was in a very tough place”.

“A major focus initially was restructuring the mobile division, which had become a significant drag on the wider group. He completely realigned it in terms of right-sizing both the store base and the cost base, and turned it from being a problem area into a positive contributor.”

Tomlinson says Baldock’s broader strategy has been to transform Currys from a “product-first retailer into an integrated services business”, encouraging customer loyalty through credit offers, delivery and installation, warranties, repairs and trade-ins.

“What is often overlooked is how much focus he placed on staff and colleagues,” he adds. “He has a mantra that customer experience can never exceed colleague experience.”

Baldock will now have to repeat that success at Boots – a brand which is desperately in need of a turnaround.

Since being folded into Walgreens Boots Alliance in 2014, Boots has endured closures, restructurings and repeated attempts to move away from its old-fashioned chemist image.

Its owners have repeatedly signalled that they would be keen to offload the British business. Walgreens launched a sale process for Boots in 2022.

However, it later scrapped the plans after failing to secure a deal at the valuation it wanted in the face of difficult market conditions and rising borrowing costs. Since then, efforts have been focused on honing the chain, including pushing through further store closures and cost reductions.

Speculation over a sell-off of the British arm was revived last year when private equity firm Sycamore Partners swooped to buy Walgreens Boots Alliance in a $10bn (£7.4bn) deal.

Shortly after the deal was completed, Sycamore split Walgreens into five standalone entities – one of which was Boots. It was seen as the first major step towards ultimately returning the British chemist to the UK stock market.

Baldock is believed by many to have been brought on to get Boots over the line for such a London listing – something insiders claim was “always the plan”. Its owners are looking for a valuation as high as £7bn. Still, some remain unconvinced that any listing would be imminent.

A senior retail industry source says his appointment is the same “as with any private equity-owned business”. “The job is to create as much value as possible for the owners,” the source says.

Given the current state of the London market, they say it is more likely that Baldock has simply been brought in to put Boots on a stronger footing. “I don’t think it’s right that he’s been brought in for an IPO.”

They say Boots’ health and beauty division is now “by far the most important part of the business”, reflecting the growing view inside retail that the future of Boots lies less in pharmacy and more in cosmetics, skincare and wellness.

That shift is already visible inside many of Boots’ larger stores, where beauty halls increasingly dominate the shop floor while traditional pharmacy space shrinks.

Boots has revamped more than 100 of its stores and updated beauty halls in more than 180 sites. It argues that this has helped it to record 20 consecutive quarters of market-share growth.

Analysts expect Baldock to continue pushing the business in the same direction because beauty products offer significantly stronger margins than dispensing medicines or selling low-cost healthcare essentials.

Jonathan De Mello, of JDM Retail, says Boots is “looking at devoting more floor space to beauty rather than distress pharmaceutical purchasing. The margins on beauty products are significantly better”.

At the same time, Boots still faces the challenge of balancing investment in physical stores with the need to boost online sales.

For all the investment Boots has poured into flagship stores and digital infrastructure, analysts argue the business still lags behind rivals on both fronts.

“The Advantage Card is strong, but the website still needs work,” says De Mello.

Former executives claim there are also still swathes of its sprawling estate which are in urgent need of investment. Renovating all of these old stores would be painfully expensive.

Clive Black, another retail analyst, agrees the chain’s estate remains uneven despite years of investment.

“There are some flagship stores where they have clearly invested heavily in beauty, but there are also an awful lot of stores around the country that look pretty tired,” says Black.

If Baldock wants to take Boots public – be it later this year or further down the line – he will have to convince investors that Boots can be a growth business rather than simply a reliable cash generator.

Black says he suspects that “Boots may end up being seen more as an income story than a pure growth story”.

Baldock will also inherit questions over Boots’ international operations.

While the retailer’s presence outside the UK may have formed part of the attraction for him personally – having steered Currys for years in both the UK and overseas – analysts suggest some international businesses could ultimately be sold off as management focuses more tightly on the chain’s strongest markets.

De Mello says Boots’ operations in places such as Germany and Mexico are underperforming. He argues the business would be better concentrating on the UK and Ireland, which he describes as the company’s “engine room for growth”.

At Currys, Baldock managed to convince the markets that physical stores still had value in the Amazon era, provided they worked seamlessly alongside a strong online offer. Between 2024 and 2026, he oversaw a tripling in the retailer’s share price.

Just last week, Baldock told The Times that he loved his role at Currys. His next move would have to be “something properly exciting to take me away from Currys”. With Boots, it seems that Baldock has found that. Now, he said, marked the start of “an exciting new chapter for Boots”.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Burnham’s bus plan leaves West Midlands with £30m bill
data.description:
Andy Burnham’s push to bring local buses under public control has left the West Midlands with a £30m bill after the private-sector operator decided to pull out of the region.

The Prime Minister hailed a move on Tuesday to transfer ownership of hundreds of bus routes, 1,400 buses and a fleet of depots from current owner National Express to West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA), which is led by Richard Parker, the Labour Mayor.

The move is part of a new “franchise” bus model that Mr Burnham is championing across the country to give local officials more control over bus networks.

However, the WMCA has ended up paying £24m and a further £5.5m over the next three years to National Express to take control of the infrastructure underpinning the network.

National Express is cutting ties with the West Midlands, where it has run buses for 40 years, after baulking at operating under Mr Burnham’s new franchise model.

The authority, comprising seven councils including Birmingham, which declared itself bankrupt in 2023, will also take over £78m in pension liabilities from National Express.

Mr Burnham hailed the deal as a “milestone” in regionalising public services and evidence of the role that No 10 North could play in supporting local leaders.

Speaking at Wolverhampton bus station, he said: “The bus service here was close to collapse. We needed to step in to secure services in the short term.

“But longer term, we are now building to a model under full public control so that people here can get the benefits of that.

“When I said we would put power back into the hands of local communities, this is exactly what I was talking about.”

A statement from No 10 did not mention the cost of the transaction or the transfer of pension liabilities.

Limits of franchising

The Prime Minister has been a vocal champion of the “franchise” system, which was introduced in 2017 and involves councils offering route franchises to the private sector.

When he was mayor of Manchester, Mr Burnham led the drive to bus franchising beyond London with the creation of the Bee Network.

However, the franchise model has been criticised for involving the costly purchase of depots and fleets.

National Express operated most of the West Midlands network under the private model introduced by Margaret Thatcher. This stripped councils of control over routes, timetables and fares and allowed private companies to run any service they wished.

While the Conservatives introduced bus franchising plans in 2017, only mayoral authorities could make the switch and Greater Manchester was alone in taking up the option.

Mr Burnham is pushing councils to make greater use of the powers.

The West Midlands agreement means National Express, which is owned by Mobico, will no longer have bus operations in the UK.

Phil White, Mobico’s executive chairman, said the sale was essential to “de-risking” the group after Mr Burnham’s franchise push threatened to heap more costs onto the company.

He said: “The uncertainty of future franchising in the area presented a significant headwind for the group in managing the cost base and liabilities of the business going forward.”

The West Midlands approved the move to franchising in May last year, with the rollout due to take until the end of 2029, which Mr White said had also created significant uncertainty.

A National Express spokesman said that despite offloading its assets, it could still tender to run buses in the Midlands when contracts are put out to tender.

data.title: Flooding to cause rail chaos
data.description:
Flash flooding is expected to cause rail chaos after weeks of drought, train bosses have warned.

Network Rail said it expected delays and cancellations because rail tracks are susceptible to being flooded when rainfall runs off dry, hard ground.

It comes after the Met Office issued thunderstorm warnings for parts of Britain on Wednesday and Thursday, warning of flash-flooding risks.

Craig Snell, a senior Met Office meteorologist, said the wetter conditions created a risk of flooding as heavy showers fell on baked, dry ground.

He said: “Parts of the North West have seen some localised flooding, and also parts of the south coast of England over the last 24 hours or so. Part of that is down to the fact that the rain is falling on quite baked ground, so the water is not sinking in like it would usually do.”

Network Rail is preparing for disruption, it is understood. Speed restrictions or suspensions are imposed on train services when flood water rises above rails, meaning storms could lead to delays and cancellations.

The Met Office said showers were expected to continue near the coast on Thursday evening, but would probably fade across inland areas overnight, with clear spells developing elsewhere.

Further showers were forecast in most parts of the UK for Friday, but were not expected to be as widespread or heavy as they were on Thursday in many areas. Some thunderstorms were also expected overnight across parts of Wales and western England.

A Network Rail spokesman said: “We are not predicting major disruption from flooding in the short or longer term this year. However, we are not complacent. 

“Our long-range forecast suggests it will be a warm, wet winter – in line with climate change predictions for Britain – and we are doing all we can to be ready for that. A programme of improving the railway’s resilience is ongoing.”

Meanwhile, a railway line on which a train derailed last week is set to remain closed until September.  A London Victoria to Eastbourne service derailed near Lewes station on Aug 13, trapping passengers in carriages. Thirty were injured, with 20 requiring hospital treatment.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) said investigators would explore whether the record-breaking spell of high temperatures and dry weather “in the weeks and months” leading to the accident had contributed to it.

On Aug 13, temperatures reached 38.1C in west London. The RAIB noted that there had been “a sustained period of hot and dry weather” before the accident. Experts said the rails at the site of the derailment had been known to be misaligned beforehand.

Network Rail and Southern Rail said the line between Lewes and Haywards Heath would remain closed until Sept 1 while the train was recovered and the track was repaired.

data.title: Guinness owner cuts 2,000 jobs as ‘Drastic Dave’ drives turnaround
data.description:
Guinness’s owner cut nearly 2,000 jobs last year as its new chief executive, Sir Dave Lewis, gutted spending.

Diageo, which also makes Johnnie Walker whisky, saw staff numbers fall by 6.4pc for the year ending June as Sir Dave launched a turnaround drive to revive the company’s fortunes.

Figures published in Diageo’s annual report on Tuesday showed it had 27,938 full-time employees in June – 1,922 fewer than the 29,860 it boasted a year earlier.

Diageo did not say how many of the jobs lost were redundancies, but it spent $514m (£380m) on redundancy payments during the year, up from $73m last year.

Sir Dave, known in business circles as “Drastic Dave” for his cost-cutting approach, has embarked on a significant overhaul of Diageo since taking charge in January.

This has included plans to find $1bn of annual savings through initiatives such as trimming duplicate head office roles across its global, regional and local teams.

The scale of the task is stark. Diageo’s revenue fell 3pc to $19.6bn last year, while operating profit plunged 27pc to $3.2bn.

The 61-year-old earned the “Drastic Dave” moniker for his cost-cutting drive at Tesco, which he led between 2014 and 2020.

During his time there, he closed stores and cut thousands of jobs as he sought to revive its fortunes.

At Diageo, he has not put a number on the jobs that will be lost in his latest overhaul.

Next year, Sir Dave stands to receive £14.25m in annual pay if he succeeds in turning the business around, according to the annual report.

His salary is £1.5m, while he can earn a bonus worth up to £3m and long-term incentive shares worth up to £9.75m under Diageo’s proposed new pay policy.

He received £1.43m for the six months he spent as chief executive during the last financial year, including a £528,000 bonus. One third of that bonus will be deferred into shares for three years.

Sir Dave said cutting spending would allow Diageo to invest in brands with greater growth potential rather than simply boosting profits through cuts.

“We’re going to double the capacity of Guinness during the course of this plan,” he said earlier this month.

Guinness sales rose 12pc last year, making it one of the few bright spots as the wider drinks market struggled.

Sir Dave has also admitted that Diageo pushed up prices too much after the pandemic, contributing to a decline in sales of its spirits brands.

“Some of the pricing through Covid-19 and thereafter has got a little bit out of whack,” he said. “What we’ve done in the last few months is take Bell’s back to where we think it ought to be, and we’ve seen a volume response.”

data.title: Bake Off bun fight triggers legal battle at Sky
data.description:
A former boss of The Great British Bake Off is suing Sky amid claims the broadcaster attempted to poach the show from Channel 4.

Letty Kavanagh, who helped make the show, claims she was fired for raising concerns about the programme’s future after Sky allegedly tried to acquire the rights to Bake Off and remove it from terrestrial TV.

Bake Off has been broadcast on Channel 4 since 2017 despite being made by Sky’s Love Productions subsidiary.

Sky is understood to have wanted the show for its own networks when Channel 4’s broadcast deal came up for renewal in 2024, although it was unsuccessful in acquiring the programme.

However, Ms Kavanagh reportedly alleged that Sky’s pursuit of the TV show was itself a conflict of interest, since – through its ownership of Love Productions – it was aware of contractual arrangements with Channel 4.

She also alleged that Sky planned to cancel some of the show’s spin-offs, such as the celebrity version and Junior Bake Off.

She reportedly claimed that this would have put hundreds of jobs at risk and would have damaged Bake Off’s brand, according to Deadline, which first reported the claims.

Ms Kavanagh has filed a legal claim at the High Court for breach of contract against Sky and Love Productions. Sky has disputed the allegation, arguing that there is no legal basis for the claim.

The Great British Bake Off is one of Britain’s most popular TV shows.

Originally broadcast on the BBC, the inaugural presenters were Mel Giedroyc and Sue Perkins, both comedians, with Paul Hollywood and Dame Mary Berry as judges.

The Channel 4 version saw Noel Fielding and Sandi Toksvig take the helm as presenters with Dame Prue Leith judging alongside Mr Hollywood.

Love Productions will soon have a new owner after Sky agreed to hand the maker of The Great British Bake Off to ITV as part of a £1.6bn mega-deal. 

ITV Studios will become a standalone production business and has secured a £2.1bn commitment with Sky for five years for shows including Coronation Street, Emmerdale, Love Island and I’m a Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!.

As part of the deal, it was announced that ITV Studios would acquire Love Productions for £200m, meaning the Bake Off producer will have a new owner.

Bake Off will return for its 17th season next month and Nigella Lawson will replace Dame Prue as a judge on the baking competition series.

A Sky spokesman said: “We do not recognise Ms Kavanagh’s account of events. We reject the possibility of a conflict of interest in relation to assets we control and wholly own and refute her allegations of discrimination and retaliation in the strongest possible terms.

“We do not intend to comment further at this stage. Regrettably, this matter is the subject of ongoing legal proceedings, in which we intend to vigorously defend our position.”

Love Productions and Ms Kavanagh’s lawyers were contacted for comment.

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Eclipse triggers plea for extra gas to support power grid
data.description:
Britain’s grid operator has issued a plea for extra gas-fired power during the solar eclipse as electricity supplies come under strain.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) said there would be a shortage of spare capacity between 5pm and 10pm on Wednesday.

It has asked gas-fired power plants to activate any additional capacity they have, saying the buffer against an electricity shortage is 1,760 megawatts (MW) below the desired amount.

Octopus Energy, Britain’s biggest electricity provider, has urged people not to use electricity during the eclipse, which will reach its maximum point at 7.12pm.

Neso said it was a “precautionary measure” because of the event.

“We have used our routine tool of issuing an Electricity Margin Notice (EMN) for tomorrow evening’s peak, which simply means we are asking market participants to make any additional generation capacity they may have available,” a spokesman said.

“The notice has been issued as a precautionary measure to the market due to the solar eclipse, and there is no risk to customer electricity supplies.”

The notice, issued on Tuesday night, is the fourth EMN the grid operator has issued this year. It said it wanted 700MW available as a contingency measure against unexpected problems.

Neso later withdraw its emergency order at 1pm on Wednesday after securing enough power. However, energy security came at a high price.

It was forced to pay up to £875 per megawatt hour for extra power supplied during the eclipse - about 10 times the usual price. Total costs are uncertain till after the event but will all be added to energy bills.

Neso said the measure did not mean that blackouts were imminent.

“An EMN is used to send a signal to the electricity market. It highlights that, in the short-term, we would like a greater safety cushion between power demand and available supply,” the notice said.

“It does not signal that blackouts are imminent or that there is not enough generation to meet current demand.”

The eclipse is expected to cut 95pc of Britain’s sunlight for a brief period, leading to a brief plunge in electricity generated by solar, which accounted for 14.4pc of Britain’s electricity last month.

It will occur during evening peak hours as people return home, turn on their lights and cook meals.

Octopus is encouraging users to switch off by offering them free electricity if they cut their usage during the eclipse.

The eclipse will first be visible in parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Russia, then enter northwestern Iberia and finish its path over the Balearic Islands at sunset, according to the European Space Agency.

The probable reduction in solar power output is significant but not large relative to overall demand.

The risk comes mainly from the speed with which light levels are expected to fall, which is much faster than in a normal sunset.

It means Neso must respond to changes in light levels much faster than during a normal sunset – with a particular focus on maintaining frequency and voltage stability.

Gas-fired generation will be key to this, as UK hydroelectric resources have been severely affected by drought-related water shortages.

Additionally, three of the UK’s 10 nuclear reactors are offline for repairs or refuelling.

Warnings in Europe

Similar warnings are also affecting Europe.

Entso-e, the Brussels-based trade body for European transmission system operators, said that the eclipse could cut Europe-wide solar output by nearly 10GW – equal to the capacity of 12 of the UK’s operating nuclear power stations.

This would “create a rapid but predictable change in generation patterns” between 7.15pm and 9.30pm central European time.

The biggest impact would be in Spain, where the eclipse could cut up to 5GW of solar generation, about 13pc of typical demand, national transmission operator Red Eléctrica said.

Meanwhile, Germany’s four high-voltage transmission operators – Amprion, 50Hertz, TenneT and TransnetBW – told Montel analysts that solar generation was expected to fall by up to 2GW, though this accounted for less than 2pc of total installed capacity.

France’s Réseau de Transport d’Électricité forecast a decrease of about 1.8GW, or around 5pc of installed capacity.

data.title: How Manchester Airport put Heathrow to shame
data.description:
On a cold, damp May morning in 2001, Sir Tony Blair, then the prime minister, cut a ribbon to open the second runway at Manchester Airport.

No one knew it at the time, but this was to be the last new runway to open in Britain to this day, testament to how inept the country has become at developing vital infrastructure.

Yet Manchester also provides a lesson in how major projects can be delivered on time and budget, not least for Heathrow, which is aiming to build Britain’s next new runway by 2035.

While Heathrow is in a different league to the northern hub – with 84 million annual passengers versus 32 million – the relative success of Manchester puts London to shame.

Astonishing as it now sounds, Manchester’s second landing strip took just four years to build and cost only £172m.

Since then, it has spent just £2bn to double the size of its main terminal and lift customer numbers by 85pc – a fraction of Heathrow’s £49bn price tag.

And while Manchester has been piling on passengers, Heathrow has lurched from one runway crisis to another while slipping down the global rankings, losing its status as the busiest airport in Europe to Istanbul last month.

Bosses are hoping to win planning permission for a third runway by 2029, with it becoming operational in 2035, but the project still faces major hurdles.

How did Manchester Airport do it? And what can Heathrow do to mirror its success?

The close ties between Manchester’s politicians and the region’s business community in the 1990s no doubt helped – in stark contrast to the rift between Heathrow and London’s mayors, from Ken Livingstone to Sir Sadiq Khan.

Graham Stringer, who led Manchester city council from 1984 to 1996, says he never understood the attitude of London politicians and some Labour colleagues to Heathrow.

“They’re damaging the London economy and the national economy by their continuing objections,” he says. “There are so many new runways in Europe in cities like Madrid, and a greater share of intercontinental traffic is now going there.

“They’ve over-responded to people who are genuinely concerned about the noise, when in reality, jets are so much quieter than in the 1960s and 70s, and the noise footprint is less and getting lower.

“They should be arguing for two new runways, not one, which gives them a heart attack when you say it.”

Stringer said Manchester’s second runway was built mainly in open countryside and attracted protests from the eco-warriors of the time, including the infamous Swampy. But a push to boost local wildlife won over sceptics.

The ownership of the airport was also divvied up between Manchester’s local district councils, where each got a small stake and a “vested interest in the airport doing well”.

Other than “some jealousy from Liverpool”, the runway also won cross-party backing across the North West and beyond, including strong support from Sir John Major’s government.

Manchester has always been good at boasting about its success, punching above its weight in garnering national attention.

But before the region’s renaissance, there was a genuine sense of malaise affecting the regions – one which leaders sought to fix.

Sir Richard Leese, who succeeded Stringer as Manchester city council chief, said council bosses were well aware of the need to put Manchester on the map after decades of decline.

He says: “We recognised that if we’re going to succeed in the modern economy, it had to be an international city and being an international city meant having good international links.

“It was also recognised that for infrastructure, if you waited until your existing assets were gone or were full, it takes a long time to build new stuff. We thought, let’s build the infrastructure in advance so that we are able to continue growing.”

Sir Richard said Manchester city council had a hand-in-glove relationship with business during the decade leading up to the airport winning planning permission in 1997.

Public-private links had been forged in the 1980s through the city’s failed Olympic bids, and as Right-leaning Labour politicians embraced projects such as the Trafford Centre.

Private capital took on an even bigger role in 2013 when local officials sold a 35pc stake in Manchester Airports Group to Australian infrastructure investor IFM.

Henri Murison, the chief executive of the Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said the step was crucial in funding terminal expansion to make full use of the space for extra flights.

“This country has lost its confidence and the thing about Manchester and the wider North is that there is no lack of confidence here,” he says. “We have the ambition and guile to get on with it.”

Although the airport’s connections with Liverpool, Leeds and Bradford will be improved by the £45bn Northern Powerhouse Rail project, approved by ministers in January, the scaling back of HS2 means the project will only run as far as Birmingham.

Murison says that while Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, indicated a substitute for the northern leg of HS2 would have to wait until the main project was completed, he expects Andy Burnham to come up with a quicker fix after long arguing that the project should not be abandoned.

He says: “I think the Government is now working on this as a project. The last chancellor said it would come in the 2040s because she didn’t have the money. But Andy Burnham has been open to using private funding.”

Lord O’Neill of Gatley has said Manchester Airport’s wealth generation backed up the argument for the fiscal devolution he advocates, and which the Prime Minister has said he intends to implement.

Writing in the foreword to a report lauding Manchester Airport’s success, he said: “The case for a second runway at Manchester was predicated on capacity and passenger forecasts. What strikes me is how much bigger the story has turned out to be.

“Places succeed when they know exactly what they’re trying to achieve and back it consistently. Manchester Airport is one of the best examples of that approach in practice.”

When Sir Tony stood on the tarmac in 2001, it was unlikely he would have foreseen the quagmire that rivals such as Heathrow would face in the future trying to repeat Manchester’s success.

But, perhaps now is the time to copy Manchester’s blueprint.
