data.title: Ovo founder in battle for control over £370m tech arm
data.description:
The millionaire founder of Ovo Energy is locked in a battle with his investors over control of the company’s £370m technology arm.

Stephen Fitzpatrick is in a standoff with Mayfair Equity Partners and Mitsubishi Corporation to determine the future ownership of Kaluza.

The dispute has emerged following the proposed £600m sale of Ovo’s energy arm to Germany’s Eon, which did not include Kaluza.

Both Ovo’s energy retail business and Kaluza are part of the broader Ovo Group, which counts Mr Fitzpatrick, Mayfair and Mitsubishi among its main shareholders.

All three have so far been united on the sale, which is awaiting regulatory approval after it was announced in May.

However, a spat has emerged over the ownership of Kaluza.

Founded by Mr Fitzpatrick in 2019 as Ovo’s software division, Kaluza was most recently valued at $500m (£370m) and was licensed to other energy companies around the world, such as France’s Engie.

The Telegraph understands that all three shareholders want control of Kaluza but agreed earlier this summer to part ways.

“They are weird bedfellows,” said one industry source. “They can’t get along. They have reached a conclusion that they need to find ways to exit this relationship.”

Mr Fitzpatrick and the investors have exchanged letters on the future of ownership of Kaluza in recent weeks, with two proposals believed to have been discussed.

One involves Mr Fitzpatrick taking control by funnelling the proceeds of the Ovo sale into Kaluza, while the other involves him stepping back in favour of the investors.

However, both sides are questioning the other about whether they have the financial firepower to take Kaluza forwards.

He is currently Kaluza’s chief executive after replacing Mel Gander in March 2026.

It is understood that Mayfair, which previously owned restaurant chain Yo! Sushi and haircare brand Tangle Teezer, would be in pole position to take control of Kaluza in the event Mr Fitzpatrick was displaced.

The investment bank Arma Partners was appointed to explore options for Kaluza last year.

All three investors are poised to make hundreds of millions of pounds from the sale of Ovo based on an existing shareholder agreement.

This will significantly increase Mr Fitzpatrick’s personal fortune after he founded Ovo Energy in 2009.

He now owns just under 50pc of the business, meaning he is in line for a potential £300m payday.

Originally set up to challenge legacy suppliers such as British Gas, the Belfast-born former JP Morgan trader turned the business into Britain’s fourth-largest gas and electricity business, serving around four million customers.

However, its growth has not been without challenges, as it previously warned about its ability to stay afloat amid regulatory scrutiny of its finances.

The Telegraph revealed this year that Ovo was cutting tens of millions of pounds in costs under a business plan aimed at securing its survival.

The Eon takeover will not only guarantee Ovo’s future but it will also create the country’s largest energy supplier with a combined 9.6 million customers.

A serial entrepreneur who modelled himself on Sir Richard Branson, Mr Fitzpatrick has also founded a string of other businesses.

They include flying taxi startup Vertical Aerospace and London’s elite private members’ club Kensington Roof Gardens.

His empire previously attracted scrutiny as he funnelled money from Ovo into his other ventures.

MPs grilled Mr Fitzpatrick about £40m worth of inter-company loans in 2022, urging him to “open the books” to shed more light on Ovo’s finances.

As well as selling Ovo, Mr Fitzpatrick also lost control of Vertical Aerospace as part of an emergency rescue deal.

In recent years, he has focused on redeveloping Kensington Roof Gardens, which has involved borrowing more than £75m from various lenders.

This includes a £15m loan subject to an interest rate of 17.5pc.

Mayfair Equity Partners, Ovo and Mr Fitzpatrick declined to comment.

data.title: Royal Navy submarine supplier weighs selling off core division
data.description:
A 143-year-old supplier for Britain’s fleet of nuclear submarines is in talks to break up its business.

Goodwin, which is making parts for the new Dreadnought nuclear deterrent, confirmed on Friday it is considering offloading a “substantial part” of its mechanical engineering division.

This includes Goodwin Steel Castings, its plant in Stoke-on-Trent, which designs precise metal components for the propulsion systems of submarines and the launchers used for Trident missiles.

Shares in Goodwin, which is valued at £1.5bn on the FTSE 250, surged by as much as 10.6pc to hit a four-month high on Friday.

The company said: “Discussions are ongoing and there can be no certainty that a transaction will be entered into.”

The company, which remains half-owned by its founding family, is a key supplier to multiple UK and US frigate and submarine programmes.

It manufactures parts for the Royal Navy’s Astute-class attack submarines and the Dreadnought programme, the UK’s £41bn fleet that will carry Trident nuclear missiles. The first vessel is expected to enter service in the early 2030s.

The sensitivities around the defence assets mean any sale could raise national security questions, with any deal and buyers facing scrutiny in Britain and the US.

Shares of Goodwin had been down 11pc so far this year after a series of disappointing results.

The company revealed in March that it had lost out on a contract to supply coastal radar antenna and transceivers in Estonia. It was also forced to request to delay the dispatch of valves to the Middle East in light of the Iran war.

Shares also fell heavily in November last year when it emerged the Goodwin family sold part of their stake.

Several buyout firms have submitted expressions of interest to the London-listed engineer in recent weeks, according to the Financial Times.

More than half of its £287m of forward orders is made up of defence contracts, which also include work to supply components for the Aukus security partnership between Britain, Australia and the US.

Goodwin’s steel castings business, which has operated since 1883, started when the family first rented an old colliery building in Hanley, Stoke-on-Trent.

It also supplies sectors including aerospace, automotive, construction, fire protection, jewellery, mining and oil and gas.

Along with its defence operations, its work has included supplying parts for the Sir David Attenborough polar research vessel.

The ship attracted global attention in 2016 after an online poll to name the vessel was won by the suggestion Boaty McBoatface. Its remotely controlled submersibles were eventually given the title.

A growing list of UK defence companies has quit the London Stock Exchange in recent years. Cobham, Ultra and Meggitt have all been taken over by US rivals or buyout funds.

Bankers at Rothschild & Co are advising Goodwin on the strategic review.

data.title: Labour’s new rules won’t fix Britain’s housebuilding crisis
data.description:
Angela Rayner claims that new planning rules introduced this week will “tackle the housing crisis”. They won’t.

Britain undoubtedly has a planning problem. But increasingly it also has a housebuilding economics problem. Developers cannot build homes profitably at the prices buyers can afford, and the Government keeps making things worse. Until they confront that, they can rewrite the planning rules as often as they like, but nothing will change.

The latest changes demonstrate this problem. Developers receive a new “default yes” for housing within walking distance of well-connected railway stations, including on some Green Belt land. That sounds like liberalisation.

But alongside these changes come minimum density requirements around and near stations, stronger protection for pubs and community facilities and a requirement for large developments to deliver at least 40pc of homes to higher accessibility standards. Green Belt developments can also face higher affordable housing and infrastructure requirements.

Taken on their own, each of these may well be defensible. We need some accessible homes. Pubs and village halls are popular. And everyone wants infrastructure improvements alongside additional housing. Collectively though, this represents a lot of additional things to load onto a system that everyone, including the Government, thinks is already too slow and too expensive.

The Government is therefore urging homebuilders to build, build, build. But only this densely, with this much affordable housing, these accessibility standards and these infrastructure contributions, while protecting an expanding list of things from development. That is not deregulation in any real sense. It is centralisation dressed up as liberalisation.

More importantly, it misunderstands why homes aren’t being built. Labour politicians have convinced themselves that if they only took on the Nimbys and changed the planning rules, housebuilders would unleash a wave of new developments. But this is only true if it makes economic sense to build new homes, and nothing in these changes tackles that at all.

A developer works backwards from the price at which a home can be sold. From that must come construction costs, finance, infrastructure, planning obligations, the price of the land and a sufficient return to justify taking the risk.

Keep adding costs, and eventually this equation stops working. The landowner can accept less, the developer can accept a lower margin or the development simply doesn’t happen.

Increasingly, it is the third option. Just 1,220 private housing sites secured planning approval in England in the first quarter of this year. In the past year, permission was granted for roughly 216,000 homes. Nowhere near the 300,000-a-year pace required to meet the Government’s ambitions.

The explanation is increasingly economic rather than bureaucratic. Materials and labour costs have risen faster than house prices, and governments have loaded on new taxes, levies and regulations. The Home Builders Federation estimates that the cost of constructing a home has increased by £76,000 since 2020, and £30,000 of this comes directly from government.

This is an industry being squeezed, not one sitting on an enormous pipeline of potential new homes waiting for Rayner to give them permission.

This matters to the Chancellor as well as the Housing Secretary. The Office for Budget Responsibility’s (OBR) current forecasts include a house-building boom that isn’t happening now – and is unlikely to happen in the near future.

The OBR scored Labour’s planning reforms as worth 170,000 additional homes in March 2025, which would lead to a 0.2pc increase in GDP by 2029-30, and lower borrowing of £3.4bn a year by the end of the forecast. The OBR left that assumption essentially intact in March this year, still pencilling in housing additions rising from 220,000 in 2026-27 to more than 305,000 by 2030-31.

But it added an unusually pointed caveat. The effect of the reforms had “yet to meaningfully materialise” in the actual data. These figures are therefore ripe for re-examination.

If the OBR looks at approvals at a 20-year low, completions forecast to fall rather than double, and housebuilders’ margins being squeezed rather than restored, and concludes that only half the promised uplift will show up, this would mean £1.7bn disappearing from the Chancellor’s headroom. If it decides the planning dividend will fail to materialise at all, that figure rises towards £3.4bn a year.

Rayner’s announcement this week gives the OBR little reason to think of anything other than a downward revision of some sort.

Britain does need to make it easier to gain permission to build. But permission is worthless if nobody can afford to build the homes afterwards.

Unless ministers start worrying less about what every new development must provide, and more about whether it is financially viable in the first place, the promised housebuilding boom will remain just that.

And come the Budget, the Chancellor may discover that the OBR forecast has a nasty housebuilding sting in its tail.

data.title: Ditching net zero would save households £540 a year, Badenoch claims
data.description:
Ditching Labour’s net zero targets could save the typical British household £540 a year, Kemi Badenoch has claimed.

A new study endorsed by the Tory leader found that scrapping construction of Scottish wind farms and connected transmission systems would save £320bn between 2030 and 2050,with the financial benefits flowing back to families.

Instead, the report, published by think tank Onward on Wednesday, said Britain should build a new generation of gas-fired and nuclear power stations across England where demand is greatest.

Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, had made wind power a key plank of his drive for a 95pc-decarbonised power system by 2030.

But Mrs Badenoch said: “Britain needs a serious plan to deal with climate change. Seriousness means looking at results, not simply setting targets and congratulating ourselves afterwards.

“Current net zero targets have driven up energy costs, weakened our industrial base, and made us more dependent on energy imports.

“Our plan means using our own oil and gas in the North Sea, removing unnecessary costs from energy bills, and backing nuclear and renewables that can provide cheap, clean, abundant energy for homes and businesses.”

Her comments prompted a backlash from Miatta Fahnbulleh, the new Energy Secretary.

Ms Fahnbulleh said Mrs Badenoch’s plan would “tie Britain to the fossil fuel roller-coaster and keep bills higher for families”.

Onward, a Westminster-based centre-Right think tank, commissioned the study from industry consultancy Transira Energy.

Its analysts compared Mr Miliband’s net zero plans with an alternative pathway focused on low costs, with a lower 80pc decarbonisation rate.

Ed Hezlet, the report’s author, said such a change would mean cutting wind farm expansion, instead boosting the UK’s fleet of 50 gas-fired power stations with new ones built mainly in southern Britain.

The UK has about 35 gigawatts (GW) of gas-fired generating capacity that Onward says should be increased to 45GW.

More than half the UK’s 55 gas plants are at least 20 years old, so such a programme would mean rebuilding or replacing them as well as constructing new ones.

This suggestion to expand the UK’s reliance on gas is highly controversial and would probably provoke a major backlash from the Government and from the many green groups campaigning against fossil fuels.

Onward argues that this would overcome the greatest cost of decarbonisation, which is the substantial expansion of the transmission grid needed to connect wind farms planned in the far north with England’s power-hungry cities – estimated to cost £137bn.

‘Renewables are not cheaper’

Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy secretary, said: “This is the most detailed costing of our electricity system that’s ever been done.

“It finishes the work I started in government that Ed Miliband cancelled – a true costing of renewables which shows they are not cheaper when you take into account their full system cost.”

However, other policy groups said wind power was still the cheapest way to create low-cost energy.

Adam Berman, the policy director at Energy UK, said expanding gas was a poor choice.

He said: “The energy sector – our members – agree that renewables, nuclear and storage are the best route to a low-cost energy system.”

Ana Musat, the policy director at wind industry trade body Renewable UK, said the UK would lose 15GW of generating capacity from its ageing nuclear and gas fleets by 2030, and that new wind was the cheapest way to replace it.

She said: “Whichever generation technology we choose, we would need new grid capacity. This doesn’t come cheap – connecting the new Hinkley C nuclear station cost £655m. But a resilient grid using a wide range of power sources is vital to maintain Britain’s energy security.”

data.title: Trump ally poised to triumph in row over London office
data.description:
Billionaire Larry Ellison has overcome opposition from neighbours to win approval for a new £100m office in Mayfair.

Mr Ellison, the co-founder of software company Oracle and an ally of Donald Trump, has won backing from planning officials to construct a new London headquarters for his science institute. The decision represents a blow to nearby Chatham House, which had raised objections.

The US tycoon’s plans involve renovating the façade of 18th- and 19th-century town houses on St James’s Square, near Piccadilly, while demolishing a 1980s rear extension at the premises. It will then be rebuilt, with the new extension featuring glass walls and terraces.

Chatham House, a renowned policy institute that owns the building next door, had raised objections, saying the project would jeopardise the secure and private environments needed for high-level negotiations and confidential discussions. 

The think tank routinely hosts heads of state, senior ministers and diplomats, and was concerned about what could be seen from the rooms of its new glass-walled neighbour.

However, planning officers at Westminster city council have recommended the office for approval in a victory for Mr Ellison. His family office bought the town houses in St James’s for £162m in 2024.

Approval comes despite an escalation of the row in recent weeks. After the tycoon’s institute, the Ellison Institute of Technology (EIT), submitted a detailed rebuttal to Chatham House’s claims, the think tank dug in its heels and commissioned an independent review of the scheme. 

The think tank argued that EIT had not carried out specific assessments of how demolition works might disrupt sensitive meeting areas.

Other nearby residents had also expressed “serious concerns” about EIT’s plans, raising questions about whether its design would fit in with the historic town houses lining the square.

Institutions raising objections include the Scotch of St James, a nearby music venue where Jimi Hendrix played his first UK gig.

While Westminster council has recommended approving the deal, the plans must still be formally voted on. They will be discussed and voted on at a council meeting on Aug 18.

The construction project is expected to cost at least another £100m, according to papers filed with the council.

Mr Ellison, who is worth an estimated $200bn (£150bn), is in talks about another major London real estate deal that would lead to Oracle moving into a new net zero office block in the City, according to property website CoStar.

The 81-year-old Oracle billionaire is a long-time ally of Sir Tony Blair, who has holidayed on Mr Ellison’s 288ft superyacht.

More recently, the world’s sixth-richest person has aligned himself with Mr Trump. The Wall Street Journal reported in June that he donated $45m to a political non-profit supporting Mr Trump’s election campaign in 2024.

EIT, Chatham House and Westminster city council all declined to comment.

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: Thames Water battling 1,000 leaks a week as heatwave bursts pipes
data.description:
Thames Water is battling at least 1,000 leaks a week as Britain’s drought crisis leads to burst pipes across the capital.

The company, which has 16 million customers, said it was racing to fix thousands of broken pipes after dry soil put pressure on its infrastructure network.

Thames said there were 2,871 burst pipes at street level last month – almost double the number in July 2025, when temperatures were lower.

The true extent of the damage is likely to be far greater, with Thames saying 95pc of water lost from pipe leaks is not visible to the public. Thames loses an average of 592 million litres of water every day in normal conditions.

The problem stems from its ageing network of pipes, which are at risk of cracking as London’s dry clay soil hardens and leads to hairline fractures in the pipes.

England and Wales suffered their driest July since records began in 1836, with nearly three quarters of England and the whole of Wales now in drought conditions.

Burst water pipes are the latest example of the extreme stress that Britain’s record-breaking heat is placing on the country.

Farmers have been left seeking emergency overdrafts from their banks because of an expected drop in crop yields this year while Britain is paying significantly more to import power from Europe after the heatwave drives up energy costs.

Temperatures are expected to soar again to 38c in parts of England on Thursday as Britain braces for its fifth major heatwave of the year.

The crisis forced Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, to chair an emergency Cobra meeting on Wednesday.

In a letter to London residents, Thames said it was struggling to cope with the scale of the damage.

“As you may be aware, we are currently experiencing a considerable number of leaks due to the long and continuing period of high temperatures,” it said.

“This prolonged period has an effect on ground conditions which impacts pipes and causes more leaks than we usually experience in a similar period of time.

“Because of this, we need to attend high-priority leaks – particularly those that impact large numbers of households – to protect our current storage levels.”

Alex Davies, a Liberal Democrat councillor in Streatham, south London, said there had been a string of leaks in the area in recent weeks.

“In my ward alone, there’s been three separate serious leaks, one of which has been going on for at least ten days now, with hundreds of thousands of litres of water lost,” he said.

“Water is quite literally just washing away while half of England is in drought.”

A spokesman for Thames Water said: “We understand residents’ frustration at seeing water escaping while temporary use restrictions are in place.

“However, leaks and bursts can unfortunately occur at any time, particularly during periods of prolonged hot weather, which can cause the ground to shift and crack, placing additional pressure on underground pipes.”

data.title: GB News investigated after guest links Pride to paedophilia
data.description:
GB News is facing an investigation by Ofcom after a guest linked Pride with paedophilia and bestiality.

The media watchdog is reviewing remarks made by Caroline Farrow for potential breaches of broadcasting standards.

In a discussion about London’s Pride parade during an episode of Alex Armstrong Tonight last month, Ms Farrow claimed the event was “not about gay rights” but had instead “become about celebrating every single sexuality that isn’t heterosexuality”.

She said this included “very bizarre and unhealthy kinks and quirks, you know, like furries and bestiality and even minor-attracted, they call themselves minor-attracted people, you know, paedophiles”.

Ms Farrow describes herself as a Catholic commentator and is a member of CitizenGO, a conservative lobby group that opposed same-sex marriage and abortion.

Her comments were condemned by Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, and attracted more than 12,000 complaints to Ofcom.

The backlash was spearheaded by the Good Law Project, a campaign group founded by Jolyon Maugham, an activist lawyer.

Matthew Gill, a lawyer for the Good Law Project, described the comments as a “hateful trope”.

Ofcom’s rules dictate that material that may cause offence must be justified by context, adding that appropriate information should also be broadcast where it would help to avoid or minimise offence.

Alex Armstrong, the presenter, challenged the comments on air, saying: “I would say the overwhelming amount of people at Pride were there for good reasons.

“I don’t think it was full of paedophiles and everything, I’m sure there are nefarious people.”

He addressed the controversy in a later episode, saying the comments were “an age-old gay trope that’s been used over a number of years to demonise and slander gay people”.

It is the latest flashpoint in a fierce row over GB News’s coverage of LGBT people.

A petition carrying more than 70,000 signatures was presented to Ofcom last year after presenter Josh Howie made comments suggesting that the gay and transgender community included paedophiles.

The regulator found that the comments were in breach of the broadcasting code but took no further action against GB News.

The broadcaster has previously insisted that it is the victim of a coordinated political attack.

Critics of the fledgling broadcaster have been ramping up pressure on Ofcom to take more action over its alleged breaches of broadcasting rules.

Mr Gill, of the Good Law Project, said: “The regulator must impose meaningful sanctions to stop this rogue channel repeating these vicious lies again and again.”

A GB News spokesman said: “These investigations have been the subject of an orchestrated campaign against GB News. As a regulated broadcaster, GB News takes its regulatory obligations seriously and complies fully with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code. 

“GB News is Britain’s Number One News Channel and has proudly occupied this position for the last 12 months. We intend to robustly defend these investigations.”

data.title: Borrowing costs surge to multi-decade highs across the West
data.description:
Borrowing costs across the West have hit multi-decade highs as traders sold off government bonds amid fears of a resurgence of inflation.

Yields rose on long-dated government debt across the US, Japan, France and Britain because of concerns that central banks would be forced to raise interest rates to tackle the fallout from the Iran war and ease inflationary pressures.

US Treasury yields climbed to 5.29pc on Monday, a 20-year high. France’s 30-year bond yield climbed to almost 4.9pc, the highest since mid-2008.

Meanwhile, Britain’s 30-year yield of 5.81pc is near a mid-May high – when borrowing costs climbed to their highest point since 1998.

Neil Wilson, an investment strategist at Saxo Bank, said: “If you see the US 30-year bond yield at the highest since 2007 and the gold price moving up quite aggressively, that’s telling you the market’s worried about inflation again.”

Prolonged uncertainty regarding the war in Iran has kept oil prices high, threatening to drive higher prices.

Traders also fear that debt-laden governments will kick off a fresh borrowing binge, and face higher interest rate bills that will stress the budget bottom line.

Matt Amis, an investment director at fund manager Aberdeen, said: “There’s definitely a jitteriness. Markets can move 10 basis points on nothing and no one really blinks, because we’re not entirely sure what’s going to happen in the back end of the year.”

‘No man’s land’

In Japan, 10-year bond yields rose by more than 0.05 percentage points to as much as 2.93pc on Monday, the highest since 1996.

The yield on 30-year bonds also climbed a similar amount to 4.06pc, near a record high posted in May.

James Bilson, an analyst at fund manager Schroders, said recent remarks by Kevin Warsh, the new chairman of the US Federal Reserve, had left the market unsure how he would tackle inflation.

“It’s not out of control, by any means,” Mr Bilson said. “He can very clearly communicate how he’s thinking, but until we hear something from him, we’re in a little bit of a no man’s land. That uncertainty is probably slightly weighing on longer-dated bonds.”

Rising yields will drive up borrowing costs for governments across the West.

In Japan, the rise comes just as Sanae Takaichi, the prime minister, tries to ramp up spending and cuts taxes to buoy the country’s struggling economy.

Economic growth unexpectedly slowed to 0.3pc in the three months to June 30, Japan’s cabinet office reported on Monday, keeping it afloat only by a 2.6pc surge in government spending.

The Bank of Japan may have to raise interest rates even as the economy slows, because the plummeting yen could trigger faster inflation and rock global bond markets.

Traders are betting that the Bank of Japan will raise interest rates again in September. The previous increase, in June, took the benchmark rate to its highest since 1995. Inflation hit 1.7pc that month, the highest so far this year.

“The BOJ and markets have seemingly grown more concerned about the risk of an inflation overshoot,” said Koichi Sugisaki, of Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities.

The bond sell-off could make it harder for Japan’s government to support its economy with higher spending and tax cuts.

The Japanese government’s debt-to-GDP ratio is already 249pc, and has barely shifted since its recent peak during the Covid-19 pandemic.

“A low-level debt crisis is already under way,” said Robin Brooks, of the Brookings Institution, a Washington-based think tank.

In a post on Substack, Mr Brooks wrote that the Bank of Japan’s bond-buying programme, which aims to stop yields rising too far, just shifted the debt problem onto the currency rather than addressing the underlying issue.

The yen hit a 40-year low against the US dollar last month. The Trump administration fears that a persistently weak yen will distort currency and bond markets, potentially driving up the US government’s own borrowing costs.

The US treasury has even sold off some of its own stock of euros to buy yen and push the currency higher. This intervention, combined with Japan’s own yen-buying, triggered a 4pc gain in the currency’s value against the US dollar. But the yen has since fallen almost 2pc as the effect of the intervention has worn off.

data.title: Your boss, your builder, your nanny – why is everyone ‘ghosting’ you?
data.description:
Seeing her 16-year-old son struggling with his computer science lessons at school, Emma did what many doting parents do: she hired a tutor to give him a weekly lesson at a cost of £70 a time. For almost two months, Emma’s son met his teacher online. He enjoyed the sessions and made significant progress. Then, earlier this year, with no warning, the instructor failed to appear for a scheduled lesson.

“My son logged on and he wasn’t there,” Emma says (she is using only her first name to preserve the privacy of her child). “My son sent a message through the portal, but received no reply. I tried to contact him as well, but also heard nothing.”

Only after she complained to the platform that facilitated the tuition did the teacher finally message to say he could no longer commit to the sessions. “I was raging. It takes a while for my son to build up a relationship with a teacher. Thankfully he took the news in his stride, but I feared it would knock his confidence and leave him wondering, ‘Was it me? Was I too difficult to teach?’ Disappearing just seemed so cowardly – especially after weeks of one-to-one contact.”

Emma and her son had been “ghosted” – and they’re far from alone. First coined more than 20 years ago as a term to describe a romantic interest who suddenly stopped calling or messaging, the act of ghosting has filtered into every area of life.

People report being ghosted by a prospective employer, a tradesperson or company that has gone infuriatingly quiet with alarming regularity, or even by a trusted figure such as a nanny or carer.

“We’re in the midst of a ghosting epidemic,” says William Hanson, the etiquette coach of The English Manner training institution. “I’m afraid we’re so overstimulated and so distracted by technology that we seem to have forgotten all about good manners.”

The workplace is where ghosting really hurts

Ironically, some of the worst excesses of ghosting are playing out in the professional world, fuelling furious LinkedIn threads about unanswered job applications, radio silence after interviews and clients who vanish after intensive pitches. Fifty-three per cent of jobseekers say they have experienced ghosting in the past year, according to a recent report by employment firm Criteria – up from 38 per cent in 2024.

Lucy Rigley, 48, a York-based graphic and digital designer, says she is increasingly ignored by potential clients. “I often travel to face-to-face meetings, and then spend hours producing bespoke quotes,” she says. While she understands that she won’t get every job and quoting is no guarantee of work, she increasingly finds her efforts – which are always at the request of a potential client – are ignored, along with any follow-ups. “It’s so frustrating [not to hear anything at all], because it takes seconds to send an email saying, ‘I can’t go ahead, thank you anyway’. I try not to take it personally, but it’s not good for your confidence or mental health.”

Rigley suspects working from home means her time is less valued, and with the pandemic shifting so much of our communication online, choosing to ignore someone has never been easier. In June, Office for National Statistics figures showed that 14 per cent of Britons still work fully remotely, with a further 25 per cent in hybrid roles.

“Lockdown encouraged us to re-prioritise ourselves. And with ghosting, you’re essentially choosing yourself over anyone else,” says Dr Marianne Trent, a qualified clinical psychologist and the host of the Psychology, Actually podcast.

Being ignored can be surprisingly damaging

Inevitably, though, not all ghosting is intentional, and much of it can be blamed on pure overload or human error. “People are often overwhelmed with all they have going on, so they might drop the ball and forget to respond,” reasons Dr Trent. “Or for those who struggle with conflict, it can be easier to say nothing than to let someone down.”

Such explanations offer little comfort to those on the receiving end, however. After launching her own business in 2019, Felicity Benn, an independent travel agent, found herself being ghosted by 60 per cent of the potential holidaymakers who had sought her out – usually after extensive work on their trips. “I spent almost a whole day on the itinerary of one couple planning a honeymoon. I held flights and hotels and arranged special extras for them. Everything was ready to go, but then it all went quiet and I never heard another word from them.”

Benn, 43, from the Cotswolds, has become far more selective about the clients she takes on nowadays, but she is still not immune to self-doubt. “It can be heartbreaking.” As Dr Trent says, our lack of control is what makes ghosting so hurtful. “It really stings, because you’re left wondering what on earth you’ve done wrong, with no feedback at all. That’s hard to take.”

For jobseekers in their later years, the reality of ghosting is especially brutal. Rob Neil was 61 when he was made redundant in summer 2024, following a career that included two board directorships and global managerial roles. Despite submitting 220 online job applications over the next six months, 90 per cent received no response. “It’s horrible. You suddenly think, ‘I started working at 17, I’ve been a taxpayer all my life, and now nobody will give me a chance.’ A couple of recruitment agencies I spoke to were at least honest and said, ‘It’s because of your age’ – even though I could work until I’m 70. Whatever happened to valuing experience?”

Neil, from south-west London, has since re-established his career in luxury homewares, but the rejection was a big wake-up call. “I thought finding work would be easy at my level. But because AI is filtering CVs, your application is unlikely to reach a human if you’re 60-plus. I’m sure the same thing is happening to university-leavers at the other end of the scale, which must be soul-destroying.”

From tradespeople to nannies, no one replies

Beyond the workplace, ghosting is perhaps most familiar in the world of home improvement. Research by the insurance firm HomeServe in 2023 found that 41 per cent of us had been ghosted by the likes of a builder, plumber, carpenter or electrician, many of whom promise to help but then evaporate. That was the case recently for Cheltenham resident Chris Fowler, who asked a local electrician to price up installation of an electric vehicle charger. He visited her home in late June, but then failed to produce a quote. Despite several calls and texts, Fowler has still heard nothing more than a month later. “He hasn’t even read my last few messages,” she says. “He was really personable, so it’s all very strange.”

A shortage of tradespeople and soaring demand from homeowners may help explain the pattern. But Dr Trent believes the rise of ghosting reflects a broader culture of instant choices and throwaway interactions. “It’s like a Tinder approach to life. We make judgments very quickly, and it’s part of that whole swipe-right, swipe-left mentality. We can be very dismissive – and in some cases, people think it’s not worth their time to respond.”

Ghosting becomes even more unsettling when it affects your family life, and in the world of childcare, the behaviour is rife. On forums such as Mumsnet and Reddit, parents describe nannies and babysitters going Awol even after establishing regular arrangements. One first-time mother was distraught when a nanny she had hired stopped turning up in her third week – despite bonding with her baby. After cancelling on three consecutive days, citing illness and transport problems, the nanny returned for a day, but then vanished again. She ignored subsequent messages and even cut off frantic calls from the mother. “I don’t usually trust people easily, but this time I did and it blew up in my face.”

For etiquette expert Hanson, such behaviour shows an erosion of personal responsibility. “As a society, we seem to have less accountability and awareness that our actions have consequences,” he says. “It’s the ostrich mentality: people think if they simply disappear, a problem will go away. But invariably it won’t.”

Even so, he believes there is hope of basic civility being restored – eventually. “I do wonder if serial ghosters will ultimately find themselves becoming the lonely ones, because people’s patience will run out. It costs nothing to give our actions a little extra thought and be more selfless, and ultimately, make the world a slightly better place.”

data.title: Britain’s vending machine goldmine that’s beating the stock market
data.description:
Luke Cassar can’t remember a time before vending machines. His mother started trading them in the late 1980s, and today, aged 32, he runs LC Vending Solutions from a single workshop in Basildon, Essex, keeping more than 150 machines stocked across offices, hotels, schools and care homes. “It’s in our blood,” he says.

It sounds like a Del Boy side hustle, the kind flogged down the pub with a wink and a handshake, but a growing band of investors say they’re having the last laugh. Running vending machine businesses pays out far more than investing in the stock market – for just a few hours’ work a week, they explain.

Some report making enough to cover the mortgage; others are thinking about giving up the day job altogether.

The numbers back them up. Britain’s vending, coffee and automated retail sector generated £3.78bn in 2025, according to the Automatic Vending Association’s annual census – growth of 3.3pc that comfortably outpaced the wider economy, which the Office for National Statistics (ONS) put at 1.4pc.

Industry estimates suggest small or entry-level vending operations turn over £6,000 to £24,000 a year at net margins of 10-15pc; mid-size make £25,000 to £120,000 at 13-18pc; and larger fleets with dozens of machines in prime locations can reach £125,000 to £500,000, where margins climb as high as 22pc.

Yet this is nothing new: the first coin-operated machines appeared in London in the 1880s, selling postcards, envelopes and writing paper.

Cassar sources machines from Spain and Italy, alongside suppliers in England, and the business covers Essex, London and the South East.

“We buy broken or damaged machines and refurbish them to sell on, bought for between £2,000 to £4,000. They can fail, though, and there are a lot of fake sellers. You can end up installing new parts, such as a card reader, which can cost £500.

“The ones we use ourselves are brand new, costing £5,000 to £11,000 depending on spec. My advice for those starting out is to buy new – you get a warranty and know they work,” he says.

He offers coffee, snack and drinks machines on different tariffs, running more than 150 across three services: managed fill-and-service (which means he comes and fills the machines himself), self-fill, and fresh bean supply for coffee. His best business is offices, where he has 38 sites, followed by factories with 22, then schools, care homes and hotels.

These hosts typically expect a cut of sales or a fixed fee in exchange for the space, electricity and footfall, ranging from between 5pc and 20pc of gross or net takings. Smaller establishments may settle for a flat rent instead.

Contracts with council-owned sites, such as railway stations, are usually won through a tender process, and the operator can agree the fee for placement within that.

“This year we’re on track to approach a turnover of £1m, with a goal of £2m within the next 18 months,” he says.

He is candid, though, that it is not a licence to print money. “Every client is different – the business is not easy.” Vending machines are his world, and he doesn’t invest elsewhere. “They’re my bread and butter, and I want to keep it like that.”

For others, a machine or two is a supplement to the day job – a slice of passive income that, once set up, largely runs itself. Many modern machines are connected, notifying the operator when stock runs low, so restocking is planned, rather than guessed at.

Daniel Egbunike, 36, from Kingston upon Thames, bought his first machine after Covid. “I wanted a business that provided a passive income,” he says. His day job is running a tiling business.

The start was chastening. A £1,000 machine bought through Facebook Marketplace failed, and he sold it on at a loss for £200. But he persevered, found a more reputable seller, and bought four machines at between £1,200 and £1,400 each.

“The next challenge was placing them. Through a friend I got a trial at the gym in Kingston University,” he says. The stock cost around £500 and lasted about a month per machine.

Cold-calling won him a care home contract, but he packed the machine with sweet treats and it didn’t work out. “I moved into offices, supplying healthier snacks, because that’s what they wanted,” he says.

He now owns 15 machines and runs his business as The Vending Stop. After buying stock, he makes around £30,000 a year. “I’m expanding, and the plan is to ditch the tiling business and do this full-time.”

Crucially, he has watched the two sides of his portfolio go head to head. “I was in the stock market before vending – crypto first, then shares. But vending performs better. With shares you grow by a percentage over time; with machines I get a set amount every month. Put £3,000 into each, and vending returns more.” He still invests £250 to £500 a month in shares, but the machines are where the money is, he says.

Joe* runs some vending machines alongside a career as a management consultant. Drawn in by the promise of passive income, the 35-year-old, from West Sussex, bought his first machine in 2021, mid-pandemic.

“I was watching all these TikTok videos of people making good money from them, and thought I’d give it a go,” he says. He paid £5,000 for a machine through Facebook Marketplace. This was steep, but it came with a location, and he made his money back in under six months.

He then went direct to a manufacturer and now owns seven refurbished machines, each costing £3,000 to £4,000 but, crucially for him, they came with warranties.

“My clients like me because I top up two or three times a week and give them a good service,” he says. “I make enough that it covers my mortgage.” After product costs he takes home around £24,000 a year – for roughly six hours’ work a week.

He is clear that maintenance must be a priority, and a key part of running a vending machine business. Machines need regassing and things break down. “Added to that, every card reader takes a fee – around 3pc per sale – off the profit line,” he says.

The art is buying stock cheaply enough to protect the margin: “I buy from wholesale provider Bookers or Amazon.”

Vending machines lose value over time, like most equipment, but usually more slowly than a car, which can lose 15 to 35pc of its value in the first year and around 50pc within three years. The bigger risk is not wear and tear but a machine going out of date. A coin-only machine is worth less now as 95pc of machines are cashless.

Tap-and-go customers are also fuelling higher profits. They tend to spend more per purchase, buying things they would have skipped if they had to find the exact change. The technology is moving quickly, too – last year’s breakout was the standalone smart fridge, a cashless, sensor-filled cabinet that charges you for whatever you take out.

There is one thing HMRC will want, though. Vending income counts as trading income, so anyone earning more than £1,000 a year – the tax-free “trading allowance” – must register for Self Assessment and declare it. That applies whether it’s a full-time operation or a couple of machines on the side.

But for vending machine investors, this is a small price to pay compared with the money that can be made. “The stock market is averaging 10pc to 15pc on broad index funds per year, versus vending returns of around 40pc to 50pc. It’s a no-brainer,” says Joe.

“The beauty of vending is simple,” Cassar adds. “If it fits, it vends.”

*Name has been changed

data.title: Sir William Jaffray, Bt, bon vivant who fought Lloyd’s of London after suffering huge losses
data.description:
Sir William Jaffray, 5th Bt, who has died aged 74, fought a quixotic and ultimately unsuccessful legal battle against Lloyd’s of London in the hope of recouping hefty losses sustained as an underwriting Name.

When he became a Name in the early 1980s, accepting unlimited liability for risks insured by syndicates in the historic City market, he believed he was joining a “sound, blue-chip institution” which would bring him a steady income with tax advantages. But Lloyd’s was riddled with malpractice, favouring insiders over “external” members such as him, and about to be hit by massive claims relating to asbestosis, hurricanes and other disasters for which it held severely inadequate reserves.

Some 34,000 Names would eventually suffer the consequences to the tune of £8bn, the vast majority agreeing to a settlement in 1996. But Jaffray led a rebel group of 216, called the United Names Organisation, accusing the institution of fraud, while being sued to pay up, potentially to the tune of £50m. It is significant that Jaffray’s favourite film was Zulu – a stand against seemingly insuperable forces.

He claimed that his cohort had been recruited on a false prospectus – that Lloyd’s was a bastion of probity and profitability when in fact its powers-that-be already knew the catastrophic scale of impending asbestosis claims and had embarked on an undeclared policy of luring new Names to spread future losses.

The case, which came before Lord Justice Cresswell’s commercial court in July 2000, was one of the largest in English legal history, lasting 20 weeks and involving 60,000 documents. Jaffray, appearing as a litigant in person, characterised Lloyd’s overall conduct as “20 years of larceny and deceit”. He accused Sir Peter Miller, a reforming 1980s chairman of Lloyd’s council, of “practised perjury” and castigated Sir David Rowland, who steered the market’s eventual rescue, for showing “no remorse or contrition for the suffering heaped needlessly upon Names”.

Jaffray’s forceful rhetoric was to no avail. The judge dismissed the charge of fraudulent representation against Lloyd’s and its council, finding that they had not concealed the extent of asbestosis losses or pursued a secret strategy of “recruit to dilute”. But he also commented on “staggering” failings and incompetence in the market, particularly among the agents who managed Names’ accounts.

Jaffray’s group refused to admit defeat, but the Court of Appeal refused their application to appeal for procedural reasons. “I am very angry,” the baronet told the press after the hearing. “It is poppycock and nonsense.”

He stated: “Let it be known abroad that our determination to obtain full and proper compensation remains undimmed. Few can deny that Lloyd’s of London is now a national disgrace, a rotten institution which replaced the principle of utmost good faith with another cornerstone in its philosophy, namely the bankruptcy of the former investors on the back of unproven and unwarrantable monetary claims.” A spokesman for Lloyd’s responded by advising the “Jaffray Names” to settle: “They have had two lengthy and fair hearings and it is time for them to draw a line.”

He declared his intention to take the unfairness claim to the European Court of Human Rights, but there were no further proceedings. His personal liability included losing Priors Dean, the Hampshire manor house he had inherited from his father.

William Otho Jaffray was born on November 1 1951, the only son of Sir William Edmund (Bill) Jaffray, 4th Bt, TD, JP, DL and his second wife Anne, the divorced wife of Sir John Worsley-Taylor, and the daughter of Captain J Otho Paget, MC, of Thorpe Satchville, Leicestershire, a legendary huntsman whose books, Memories of the Shires and Hunting Reflections, were republished in the 2010s.

The Jaffrays were originally from Stirling in central Scotland. John Jaffray moved to Birmingham and was involved in almost every aspect of Birmingham life – the Liberal party, hospitals, institutes, libraries, the Birmingham Joint Stock Bank and the founding of the Birmingham Daily Post and the Birmingham Daily Mail. He was created a baronet in 1892.

Sir William’s father, Sir John’s grandson, had been an outstanding sportsman and a keen rider to hounds in North Warwickshire, despite having lost an arm in the First World War. He died in 1953, so Will succeeded shortly before his second birthday.

Will was brought up at Priors Dean, near Petersfield in Hampshire, in a family of three women of strong character. His Paget grandmother, to whom he was devoted, lived in the neighbouring cottage and hoped he would meet a nice “gal” at a hunt ball. With his formidable mother (who had worked at Bletchley) he had a complicated relationship.

She kept the house going for him against all odds, but when he came of age, she had to leave, at which point she went to court claiming compensation of £250,000. After years of intense litigation, mother and son resumed close relations and Will was her devoted companion when she was in her 90s. She died aged 101. His half-sister, Annette Worsley-Taylor, who ran the London Designer Collections, was not averse to issuing him robust advice.

There was nothing in Will’s early life to suggest he would be such an organised and forensic attacker of Lloyd’s. He had passed through Eton without academic distinction. He had tried many enterprises, including dealing in art, without settling into any fixed career. In the words of the Leonard Cohen song, he was always seeking that card that was “so high and wild” that he would never have to deal another. Interviewed for a position at Saatchi and Saatchi, he was transparent in his expectations – the chance to meet beautiful models, preferably on overseas shoots.

As a teenager at Priors Dean, his half-sister and her friends had thought it amusing to suggest that the au pair had taken a liking to him. Encouraged, he went up to her room. Their joke misfired when he did not immediately emerge. His interest in girls was fuelled in the hedonistic days of the 1970s and nurtured through all subsequent decades. A good-looking man, unrestrained by the inhibitions that haunt many reserved Englishmen, he was refreshingly direct. He never promised them a rose garden. When asked how he coped with the conventional restrictions of matrimony, his reassuring reply was “Why go to the pub for a beer, when champagne is flowing freely in the house?”.

He was tenacious, flirtatious and one of life’s bon vivants. Any aspiring playwright would have welcomed him in the audience for his loud and generous laugh (which also made him a conspicuous figure in London restaurants). He inspired loyalty in his friends, which he totally reciprocated. As was written of his father, he showed “unstinting friendship, indomitable cheerfulness and unquenchable courage”. 

He was the first to offer solace to a friend in need. He was forever game for adventure. Recovered from a guest’s flat after a pyjama party on a cold morning in November 1975, he stepped out of the car in Sloane Square, pyjama-clad and unshaven, and purchased a Remembrance Day poppy for £5 from an astonished Chelsea lady outside Peter Jones.

He was first married in 1981, to Cynthia Ross Corrington, a beautiful Canadian who had worked at Christie’s. They had three sons and a daughter, but divorced in 1997. After losing his house in the Lloyds fiasco, he wound up in lodgings in Camberwell. He had enjoyed President Nixon’s line: “Only if you’ve been in the deepest valley can you ever know how magnificent it is to be on the highest mountain.” 

While in his dark valley, he rarely saw his friends, but on meeting his second wife, Constance Haynes Latshaw, whom he married in 2009, that changed. He found himself living in her fine apartment in Eaton Place, London, and spending part of the year with her in Nevis. She even flew his mother to the Caribbean for holidays. They were generous hosts. However, they divorced in 2018.

In his long illness, he again emulated President Nixon. He was not a “quitter”. One minute he was attached to tubes in Charing Cross Hospital at the brink of death, the next back in his flat and shopping on his own. As recently as this May, back in hospital and seemingly in extremis, he married Gowri Siva, a former lawyer who founded Art Fancier, arranging bespoke artistic tours.

They had known each other since 2023. He enjoyed the response of one friend: “It was entirely in character that you should get married without your trousers on! You are the keeper of the flame.” She looked after him in his last days. He will be buried next to his parents in the churchyard of his beloved Priors Dean.

He is succeeded as 6th baronet by his son Nicholas, born in 1982.

William Jaffray, born 1 November 1951, died 11 August 2026

data.title: Boots in £7.5bn sale talks with billionaire family behind Primark
data.description:
Boots is in talks to sell itself for £7.5bn to the family behind Primark and an Australian pharmacy chain.

The billionaire Weston family, which owns Primark, is weighing up a bid that would see the chemist scrap plans for a London listing, according to the Financial Times.

The retail giant is understood to be in talks alongside Sigma Healthcare, an Australian pharmacy group, about a possible takeover of the 177-year-old chemist from Sycamore Partners, its private equity owner.

A takeover of Boots would derail plans for a stock market listing. The recent appointment of Alex Baldock – the former Currys boss credited with turning around the electronics retailer – as chief executive had fuelled speculation that Boots was being prepared to join the London Stock Market. 

Insiders had previously suggested that a flotation valuing the chain at up to £7bn was “always the plan”.

News of the talks came as Boots revealed that profits jumped by a quarter to £337m last year, as demand for weight-loss jabs, vaccinations and beauty products helped drive sales growth.

The Westons are one of the world’s richest retail families. Through their sprawling business empire they already control Primark-owner Associated British Foods (ABF), as well as Fortnum & Mason and major supermarket and pharmacy chains in Canada.

A deal would also deepen the family’s ties to British retail just months after it unveiled plans to split Primark from ABF, ending a six-decade partnership between the fashion chain and the conglomerate’s food operations.

Sigma, meanwhile, is a fast-growing Australian healthcare group best known for its links to Chemist Warehouse, Australia’s largest pharmacy retailer.

It has recently signalled ambitions to expand internationally and only last month entered the UK market through a pharmacy joint venture in and around London.

Hundreds of stores closed

A sale of Boots has been talked about for years. Walgreens first tried to offload it in 2022, before abandoning the effort when bids failed to meet expectations.

Sycamore Partners revived expectations of a breakup when it bought Walgreens Boots Alliance last year and carved out Boots as a standalone unit.

Boots has spent the past two years trying to improve its attractiveness to potential bidders. 

It has closed hundreds of under-performing UK stores as part of a broader cost-cutting drive, including a programme to shut branches, trimming its footprint from about 2,200 stores to roughly 1,900 in 2024.

At the same time, the chain has benefited from a boom in private healthcare services and a push into premium beauty brands, with online sales also rising sharply as more shoppers turned to its app and delivery partnerships.

The Weston family already has a presence in the pharmacy sector through Shoppers Drug Mart, a Canadian chain with more than 1,300 locations that it acquired in a multibillion-pound deal more than a decade ago.

Boots declined to comment.

data.title: Virgin Atlantic and Trainline accused of tricking customers on pricing
data.description:
Virgin Atlantic and Trainline are facing an investigation over claims they tricked customers into paying over the odds with misleading pricing.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it was concerned that customers were not shown the true upfront cost of buying package holidays and train tickets.

The regulator is also examining similar concerns of so-called drip pricing at Red Driving School.

Drip-pricing is a practice in which mandatory charges are separated from the headline price and added later in the buying process.

This can trick consumers choosing to book with one company over a rival and leave them facing unexpected costs at the checkout.

The CMA said consumers could be entitled to compensation if it is found that the companies broke the law.

It comes as part of a wider clampdown by the competition watchdog over misleading pricing practices.

The CMA said: “Such practices can also impact competition between businesses, as a firm using drip pricing may falsely appear to be cheaper than a competitor and attract more customers.”

The Trainline investigation is focused on whether all mandatory fees were displayed upfront to travellers buying train and coach tickets in advance, on its app and website.

The CMA said it observed transactions with additional fees ranging from 50p to £2.79, with a £1.50 booking fee for coach journeys. Shares in Trainline dropped 14pc in early trading.

The investigation into Virgin Atlantic is looking into whether mandatory resort fees and local taxes for package holidays were properly disclosed.

Red Driving School is being investigated over how a mandatory booking fee and a so-called digital fee – typically £7 per booking – was displayed for driving lessons.

Emma Cochrane, executive director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: “Clear pricing helps people compare offers confidently and choose the option that works best for them.

“Unexpected mandatory charges make this much harder.”

A spokesman for Virgin Atlantic Holidays said: “We take our responsibility to customers incredibly seriously and we always want to ensure they can make an informed decision when booking a holiday with us.

“Mandatory fees are indicated at multiple stages throughout the booking journey. We are reviewing the points raised by the CMA carefully and will co-operate fully with its investigation.”

A Trainline spokesman said: “Trainline is committed to offering customers a transparent booking experience with clear pricing and genuine value.

“We’ve proactively engaged with the CMA over several months and we are taking proactive steps to enhance how certain fees are presented to our customers.

“We will continue engaging with the CMA to address their questions.”

Red Driving School was contacted for comment.

data.title: Guardian staff revolt despite above-inflation pay rise offer
data.description:
The Guardian has been plunged into a fresh row over pay despite staff being offered an above-inflation increase.

The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) has rejected the newspaper’s pay offer of 3.85pc, saying it did not “meaningfully” address cost of living pressures or reflect increased workloads.

That is despite the consumer prices index plus housing – a measure of inflation used by the company to set pay rises – standing at 2.8pc.

A meeting between the NUJ and the company is scheduled through the Acas mediation process next month.

The NUJ has been locked in a lengthy dispute with The Guardian since the company offered staff a 3.78pc increase in March.

The union unanimously rejected this offer, which was linked to the average inflation rate for the 12 months to February. It then rejected an improved 3.85pc proposal, saying this would add only £36,000 to the total wage bill.

Union bosses claimed the sum would amount to a real-terms pay cut for hundreds of staff in order to fund a small cost of living payment worth around £200 a year for lower earners.

The NUJ also aimed at a proposed 3.6pc increase for freelancers and casual workers, branding it a “provocative move” as the media group also reviews their working terms.

It marks the latest in a string of disputes at The Guardian amid simmering discontent over the leadership of editor-in-chief Katharine Viner.

Journalists staged a 48-hour walkout in 2024 over the sale of The Observer to media start-up Tortoise, which they branded a “betrayal”.

Bosses pushed ahead with the sale of the Sunday title even after the strike, which was the first in more than half a century.

Staff have since outlined a litany of grievances, including a website redesign last year and extra work caused by a strategy called Project Berger, which includes greater focus on audio and video and an aggressive expansion in the US and Australia.

The NUJ said the latest pay offer failed to reflect the increased workload since the sale of The Observer and the extra demands on staff created by Project Berger, which is being funded by a £13m drawdown from the Scott Trust endowment.

The union argued that the media group could afford a more generous salary increase given revenues grew 7pc last year and are expected to grow by a similar amount in the year ahead.

In an email to members, the NUJ said: “We are still loss-making, but this is because the company has chosen to invest for growth. We support that.

“We also believe staff should keep a share of the growth they have helped to create.”

A Guardian spokesman said: “We have put forward a fair and industry-leading pay offer that reflects our commitment to supporting staff during a challenging economic period.

“Throughout negotiations, we have expressed our willingness to work with the NUJ on how this offer could be structured to best support lower-paid colleagues. We remain committed to constructive dialogue through Acas.”

data.title: Senior Russian banker sacked after saying: ‘We’re losing to Ukraine’
data.description:
A senior Russian banker has been sacked after telling a public meeting that Russia is losing the “war of attrition” in Ukraine.

Andrei Klepach, the chief economist at state-owned lender Vnesheconombank (VEB), was fired after the bank’s bosses received a “call from above”, according to independent Russian news site The Bell.

Mr Klepach had told a meeting at the Moscow Exchange’s Nikitsky Club that the war’s effect on Russia’s economy risked plunging the country into a “social crisis”.

“We’re falling behind,” Mr Klepach said, according to remarks first reported by The Moscow Times. “We’re losing both the technological and economic competition globally. We’re losing not only to China and the US, but in some ways, we’re losing to Ukraine.”

He added that while the Ukrainian economy was “partially destroyed”, it had continued to endure.

“In this war of attrition, we will not win the competition,” he said. “We’re under the illusion that everything [in Ukraine] will collapse. It hasn’t, and it won’t. Meanwhile, the costs we bear are mounting.”

These costs included rising inequality, deteriorating healthcare, and “uneven development” in science and technology.

“A social crisis could emerge, and when no one particularly expects it. But let me remind you, no one expected the February Revolution either,” he said, referring to the Communist uprising of 1917.

“I don’t believe Russia will collapse, but I’m almost certain that we’ll end up in a social crisis.”

A spokesman for VEB told The Telegraph that Mr Klepach “no longer holds the position of chief economist”.

The spokesman said: “A new candidate will be appointed to this position soon, and the candidate has already been selected.”

Mr Klepach’s remarks, which were delivered in May but first reported in the weekend, clash with the Kremlin’s official stance on the state of the Russian economy.

Vladimir Putin has refused to acknowledge Russia’s lack of progress in the war, nor its increasing toll on the country’s financial health.

Official data released last week suggested Russia’s gross domestic product expanded 1.3pc in the second quarter from a year earlier, up from a 0.2pc contraction in the first three months of the year.

But Liam Peach, a Capital Economics analyst, said in a note that Russia’s economy was likely to “stagnate for the foreseeable future”.

The country is grappling with fuel shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone attacks, which have targeted Russian refineries.

The economy is surviving on higher global oil prices driven by the war with Iran and heavy spending on manufacturing weapons.

Mr Klepach said while Ukraine was suffering a “demographic disaster”, it was “despite everything, surviving” – largely because of Western financial aid.

The economist is a high-profile, influential figure in Russian economic circles. Before joining VEB in 2014, he was a senior official at Russia’s economic development ministry, rising to deputy minister in 2008.

data.title: Burnham faces two big tests on the economy
data.description:
Andy Burnham’s claim to being a broadly pro-business Prime Minister faces two important tests in the coming months.

One is the decision on whether to give the Rosebank and Jackdaw North Sea oil and gas fields the go-ahead.

From an economic perspective, this is a no-brainer. If economic growth were the priority, Burnham would indeed go further and like Norway max out on all that’s left beneath Britain’s sovereign waters. That won’t happen, so we must settle for Rosebank and Jackdaw.

By giving the North Sea a longer shelf life than it otherwise would have, Burnham not only supports jobs and tax revenues, but – contrary to what environmental lobbyists claim – helps ensure a smoother and less disruptive progression to the prescribed goal of an all-electric economy.

In a recent article, Lord Howell, a former UK energy secretary, pointed out that finding enough power for 13 new data centres under construction, and up to 71 more waiting in the queue, will be challenging enough. Converting the great hinterland of existing energy consumption to electrons comes on top.

There are limits to what wind and sun can provide, so the power must inevitably come from a combination of new-build nuclear and gas-fired generating plants. “We shall need every therm of gas we can release from the North Sea – and oil too, imported and local – to fill demand,” says Lord Howell.

So which is it to be? The rigidly imposed and economically costly requirements of climate change mitigation or a pragmatically driven, common-sense approach that promises a less disruptive transition to a greener future?

The other test is whether to face down demands for higher taxes on banks to fund the Government’s various spending priorities or to give in to the siren calls of those who see the City as just a rich source of taxation there for the fleecing.

Heavy lobbying from the City has thus far seen off the threat, but with a new Prime Minister comes a renewed assault. The banks are making substantial profits, in part at the expense of the taxpayer via the interest they receive on their holdings of central bank reserves, so why not claw some back?

Here’s why. It’s called killing the goose that laid the golden egg, and though not in itself a terminal blow, it would further add to the steadily accumulating list of reasons for international capital not to choose London as its home.

One of the redeeming features of the Tony Blair/Gordon Brown period of government is that they did at least grasp how important the City was to the economy and to tax revenues, and loosened the leash accordingly.

It was a kind of Faustian pact; the City would pay for Labour’s social objectives, and in return, the City would be given free rein to do largely what it liked.

By then, the great manufacturing dynamo on which the British Empire had been built had long since dimmed. In its place stepped finance as Britain’s pre-eminent economic force, turbo-charged by the Big Bang capital-markets reforms of the Thatcher years and a fast globalising international economy whose needs the City came to serve.

In came the Americans, and in too came the European banks, most of the latter choosing to consolidate their capital markets activity in London away from the dead hand of home nation governments.

As an industrial strategy it certainly had its shortcomings as well as its casualties, but it sort of worked. Until, that is, it didn’t. In 2008 the whole edifice imploded, and the Government’s cash geyser dried up.

The City eventually clawed its way back from the catastrophe of the global financial crisis, but it never truly recovered the grandeur of its glory years.

Tipping points are always hard to identify until it’s too late, but my sense is that we are quite close to one as things stand. Admittedly, this has been said many times before of the City, particularly around the time of the referendum on leaving the EU, but thus far it has defied predictions of post-Brexit decline.

The number of jobs relocated to rival European centres since Brexit is so small that nobody any longer bothers to track them, and cumulatively is certainly nowhere near what was widely forecast at the time.

The European Commission has meanwhile pretty much given up on its determination to bring clearing of Euro-denominated interest-rate derivatives back to Paris and Frankfurt. If London were banned, European banks warned, they’d take the business not to rival European financial centres but to New York, which, unlike the City, has designated “equivalence” for regulatory purposes.

City interests were badly neglected during Brexit negotiations with the EU, much to the amazement of European negotiators who couldn’t understand how their British counterparts could treat such a tax-rich industry so casually.

“F--- business”, Boris Johnson reputedly said in response to a growing chorus of complaint, but his supposition that the City could take care of itself proved reasonably well founded.

Unfortunately, there is also only so far you can push things before the wheels start flying off, and the banking surcharge – though not a particularly big deal in the scale of things – may be the final straw.

This was cut from 8pc to 3pc by the last Tory government in an effort to restore lost tax competitiveness, but it still leaves the overall rate on banking profits well above the European average.

It is true that banks have significantly contracted their lending to small and medium-sized enterprises in recent years, yet the problem is as much lack of demand as supply. Bitter experience has taught SMEs not to put themselves in hock to the hot money of the City.

Banks could theoretically correct this situation by force feeding the market with credit, but since the financial crisis there are major regulatory constraints on this kind of “going for growth” balance sheet expansion. Almost invariably, it ends badly.

In any case, if credit expansion is the Government’s aim, it is scarcely helped by taxing its providers more. At a time when London’s stock market already seems to be in almost terminal decline, this further act of economic sabotage at the heart of the City could be the final straw, if only for its signalling of a country that is turning its back on its most successful industry.

New figures by the Office for National Statistics this week showed that in the three months to the end of June, private-sector wage growth slowed to a level that barely kept pace with the rate of inflation. Public-sector wage growth on the other hand was still racing away at 6.1pc.

For how much longer can the Government keep flogging the City workhorse to pay for its public sector largesse? For finance, there are greener pastures elsewhere to graze on.

data.title: Founder of failed Chinese property giant sentenced to life in prison
data.description:
The founder of failed Chinese property giant Evergrande has been sentenced to life in prison after his business’s collapse rocked the country’s housing market.

A court in Shenzhen ruled that Hui Ka Yan, once Asia’s richest man, had committed “multiple crimes”, including bribery, fraud and embezzlement.

Judges ordered that his personal assets be seized, while Evergrande itself was fined around 15.82bn yuan (£1.73bn) for crimes including falsifying records and concealing debt.

More than 50 other people connected to the firm, including Hui’s two sons, Xu Zhi Jian and Xu Teng He, were also sentenced, according to state media reports.

Prosecutors said Hui, who pleaded guilty in April, had acted as the true power behind Evergrande and had broken the law by inflating the company’s assets and hiding its debts between 2016 and 2021.

It marks a dramatic rise and fall for a man who grew up in poverty in China’s Henan province.

The son of a woodcutter, Mr Hui abandoned a job in the steel industry in 1992 to begin a career in property development, eventually founding Evergrande in 1996.

At its peak, Evergrande commanded a stock market valuation of more than £37bn with more than 1,300 developments across some 280 cities, diversifying into ventures such as football and electric vehicles.

However, much of its rapid expansion was funded with borrowed money. When Beijing tightened rules on property lending in 2020, Evergrande’s access to credit dried up.

The business offloaded properties at hefty discounts in an effort to pay off its debts, but defaulted on its loans in 2021. It has since been forced into liquidation.

As one of China’s biggest property companies, Evergrande’s collapse was widely blamed for triggering a slump in the country’s housing market.

The contagion from its collapse spread to other Chinese property companies, which then faced their own financial struggles.

In April, the Shanghai court heard that Evergrande had collected millions from people who had paid in advance to buy new homes.

However, that money was not used to build those properties but was instead used to bankroll other construction projects, leading to hundreds of unfinished sites.

Mr Hui has been held under surveillance by the Chinese authorities since 2023. In 2024, he was banned from China’s capital markets for life.

The scandal has also ensnared Evergrande’s auditor, PwC, which has been fined by both mainland Chinese and Hong Kong regulators.

Evergrande’s liquidators also brought a £6bn negligence claim against PwC and its Chinese and Hong Kong branches in May.

Lawyers for PwC’s global business have argued that its Chinese and Hong Kong divisions are separate businesses and it should not be a defendant.
