data.title: Eclipse pushes Britain’s power bill to £6.2m
data.description:
Britain’s grid operators had to pay £6.2m for extra electricity to keep UK lights on the day of the solar eclipse.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) had to pay gas-fired power stations premium rates for supplies as it scrambled for extra power on Wednesday.

It was forced to pay £6.2m for the extra power – 63pc more than the £3.8m spent the previous day, when conditions were similar but without an eclipse – with the costs ultimately added to bills.

Most of the payments went to just two power stations whose owners stepped in with offers of extra power once prices had risen.

Seabank power station in Bristol, co-owned by SSE, was paid up to £890 per megawatt hour (MWh) for pledging extra power – about 10 times the normal rate for wholesale electricity.

Similarly, Uniper was able to demand up to £739 per MWh for power from its Connah’s Quay plant in Wales.

Neso also had to import extra power from Europe via subsea interconnectors to keep the UK system stable.

At one point during the evening, it had to breach limits imposed by the EU to stop the UK’s growing reliance on the system from disrupting EU power markets, according to analysts.

Neso’s problem in dealing with the eclipse was not the reduction in solar output itself – which was small compared to overall demand – but the speed with which it happened.

It meant Neso had to be able to respond to changes in light levels much faster than during a normal sunset, with a particular focus on maintaining frequency and voltage stability.

The rarity of such events also made it hard to predict how demand would be affected.

Kathryn Porter, from energy consultancy Watt-Logic, said the event and the reliance on power from Europe showed how Neso was struggling to control the grid.

She said: “Most of the imported power would have come from gas and coal fired power plants in other countries, showing our continuing reliance on fossil fuels.”

The struggles of Neso’s control room to keep the UK power system in balance contrasted with the scenes in parks, on commons and on hillsides across Britain as millions of people enjoyed a once-in-a-lifetime solar eclipse that darkened skies across Europe.

UK eclipse watchers saw – at best – a 95pc eclipse, so the sun was never completely covered.

However, Iceland and northern Spain had the full experience, witnessing the Continent’s first total solar eclipse in 27 years.

A Neso spokesman said the request for extra generation capacity prior to the eclipse was “a routine and precautionary step which proved prudent and effective.”

He added: “Great Britain has one of the most reliable electricity systems in the world, operating at 99.999pc reliability. NESO continues to manage the system in real time to keep electricity flowing safely and securely.”

data.title: The green transition will fail if it takes us to the Chinese begging bowl
data.description:
Want to make something in Britain? You’d better be amazing and innovative, because you’re a jockey carrying extra weight. British factories pay around four times as much for their electricity as their Chinese rivals, and about double our European friends. That alone explains so much of what’s wrong with our economy, and so much of what it would take to put right.

It’s also the missing element from the ever-brilliant Tim Stanley’s column in these pages on Sunday. The question for us as Conservatives isn’t whether the climate is changing, we can see that for ourselves. The question is: what we should do about it?

How do we adapt our economy quickly enough to have the electrical power we need to innovate and adjust to a new world? How do we make sure we have a stake in that future and not just the legacy of our past?

If we get that wrong, Britain will go from the cutting edge of scientific leadership, to economic vassalage. The trouble is, that’s exactly where the policies so many of the so-called environmentalists would take us, costing not just Britain but the world.

Let’s start with the numbers. Britain emits a little under half the carbon we did in 1990. That may sound like a triumph, but the carbon in what we actually consume, imports included, has fallen by only about a fifth. That gap isn’t a saving, it’s a transfer. Worse, while we’ve exported the jobs, we’ve increased the carbon.

A kilowatt-hour on the Chinese grid carries around three times the carbon of one here. A blast furnace emits about two tonnes of carbon for every tonne of steel, nearly five times what the electric-arc furnace now being built at Port Talbot will emit. Again and again we’ve priced British carbon to punish, pushed the work overseas and raised the total emitted.

It’s almost as though we believed that net zero in one country alone, and that a country responsible for less than 1 per cent of global emissions, could fix it alone. It won’t. What’s worse, this is a bet against the future and a punishment of innovation.

Almost every technology in the green transition has British fingerprints on it. The cathode at the heart of every lithium-ion battery in the world was discovered in an Oxford laboratory in 1980, winning its inventor a Nobel Prize. Perovskite laid over silicon, the most efficient solar architecture yet built, came out of an Oxford spin-out, and graphene was isolated in Manchester in 2004.

That last discovery tells a story. A British innovation that has generated interest in China so that more than half the connected patents are there. It’s true that China has dominated the development, but if we’re priced out of the innovation, there’s no carbon-free future.

That’s even true at sea. The 108m blades turning on Dogger Bank are cast in Hull, more than 2,500 of them since 2016, including the first recyclable blades in the world. But every rise in the price of power raises the cost of the next idea, and sends the factory that would have built it somewhere else. Everything that costs our economy makes the future more carbon-fixed.

None of this is an argument against batteries, wind or solar. We know that a perovskite panel repays the carbon spent building it within months and then generates for 25 years. It’s an argument about where panels are made.

These have moved to Germany, others to China, but every factory we shut here reopens somewhere the energy is cheaper and that often means coal. How is that decarbonising anything except our consciences? We’ve worshipped net zero and exported the jobs, raised the costs, and the atmosphere has sent us the bill anyway.

That’s just the science. Now for the politics.

Dependency of this kind doesn’t stay commercial. For years many have complained about dependency on the Gulf for our energy, the costs needed to patrol those seas and guard those ports and Saudi Arabia controls about 10 per cent of global oil. China is in a league of its own making over 80 per cent of the world’s solar modules and battery cells, and refining about 90 per cent of its rare earths.

And we know Beijing is thinking about the power in both senses. Last year, they restricted exports of heavy rare earths and the magnets made from them, then tightened the regime again this year against Japan. Loosening and tightening the tap so that no rival supply chain ever reaches competitive scale is about control not commerce.

That’s where the politics of punishment take us, not to the green fields, but to the begging bowl. Britain needs a better choice. We’re lucky to have it.

We can innovate with cheap nuclear at scale so that each small modular reactor isn’t a novelty but a simple permitted development; that would generate export options and deliver more options for innovators. Pumping gas from beneath our own seabed, rather than shipping it through straits Iran can close, would allow that bridge to the future to be built as affordable power keeps the lights on in universities and startups around the country.

And stripping the levies off industrial electricity and breaking the pricing rule that ties every unit of cheap British wind to the most expensive molecule of imported gas would free manufacturers to compete with coal-powered rivals.

Tapping North Sea gas and building nuclear plants isn’t about freezing in a carbon economy but powering our transition. We can choose to invest in the different choices of nuclear, solar and wind but only with cheap energy can we afford to make that change. That’s what Conservative environmentalism should be about: grounded in national interest, economic reality, and scientific fact.

The real answer to Tim’s challenge is more. More power, more ideas, more manufacturing, so that we finally get to less: less carbon, less dependency, less job loss. That’s why we need to be honest with the science and the politics. Take the weight off the jockey and we can win the race.

data.title: The chart that proves it’s Labour killing employment
data.description:
The social media whizzes at Number 10 had probably already prepared the smug TikToks celebrating “good growth in every postcode”. And the Chancellor had probably already composed a self-congratulatory post or two about how his Government was delivering a rapid recovery. The markets were confidently expecting a significant fall in the rate of unemployment when the figures were released this morning.

There was just one catch. The numbers turned out to be dreadful – and, even more seriously, they were only going to get worse over the next few months.

In the three months to June, the unemployment rate remained stuck at 4.9 per cent. That was bad enough in itself, given that some dire numbers from last year dropped out of the calculations, and we should have been seeing an increase in summer holiday work, as well as the impact of the World Cup.

Dig into the numbers a little, and the figures were even worse. In total, the number of payrolled jobs fell by 13,000 in July, following another 13,000 fall in June. A net total of 94,000 jobs have been lost over the last year, and 188,000 over the last two years. The number of vacancies fell yet again, down by another six thousand. The chart below is striking, and a damning indictment of Labour.

Crucial sectors such as retail were hammered, with 75,000 jobs in the sector disappearing. And wage growth slowed dramatically, down to less than 3 per cent, unless you happen to be lucky enough to work in the public sector of course, in which case your wages were still rising by more than 6 per cent a year.

Add it all up, and the conclusion is clear. Britain’s labour market has started to slow dramatically. It has not yet collapsed, but it is getting close to the point where it will.

It is not hard to figure out why. The slow-motion car crash of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves’s decision to hike the rate of National Insurance paid by employers is still playing itself out. No one fires people on the day the tax on jobs goes up.

Instead, they wait for them to leave and don’t replace them (it’s a lot easier than risking an expensive tribunal). The living wage has been pushed way ahead of the rate of inflation, and certainly way ahead of output, so it is now above the point where it is worth hiring people.

Angela Rayner’s extra employment rights for workers may be well-meant, but as they start to bite they have also made employing someone far riskier, especially for the small businesses that account for the bulk of job creation.

Soaring rates, green levies, and the highest energy prices in the developed world have also forced many businesses to close, with the staff laid off at the same time. All of this combined means the labour market is starting to break.

It is only going to get worse over the next few months. The ban on zero-hours contracts will trigger another round of job losses, as some employers can’t afford to offer full-time positions instead, while rising inflation, and yet more tax rises in the Budget, will crush demand and confidence.

As vacancies fall, and fewer people have jobs, they have less money to spend, and that makes it even tougher for the businesses that remain open. Britain has had plenty of economic problems for at least two decades. But at least it used to generate lots of jobs, even if they were not always well paid enough, or in high-growth industries.

Under Labour, that is no longer true. Andy Burnham’s new government doesn’t appear to have a clue what to do about it.

data.title: Greens call for inquiry into ‘culture and behaviour’ of media
data.description:
Zack Polanski has demanded an inquiry into the “culture and behaviour” of the press, adding that it was time the media was “sorted out”.

The Green Party leader signed a letter to Andy Burnham demanding the Government launch an inquiry into how to “ensure a responsible press” following Jason Arday’s death.

He has also described the Independent Press Standards Organisation (Ipso) regulator as “toothless” and called for the forced sell-off of most national newspapers by banning foreign ownership.

His intervention comes as Green Party members called for the Government to reopen the Leveson inquiry to ensure its “full completion” and to place the media under a “genuinely independent and recognised regulator with effective enforcement powers”.

Green members put forward the motion that would also see a new regulator “map and address” examples of racism and ableism and monitor “harassment” allegedly arising from news stories.

The motion was put forward two days after Mr Arday’s death and before the Greens’ conference in October, where it could become party policy if approved by a majority of members.

Mr Arday, who was Cambridge University’s youngest-ever black professor, was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday.

The 41-year-old had resigned from his position as professor of sociology of education the week before, citing the “unrelenting level of public scrutiny” following accusations of plagiarism and the university launching an investigation into his appointment.

On Saturday, Mr Burnham paid tribute to Mr Arday, whose death he described as a tragedy. He also called for a “moment of reflection” and urged people “not to rush to judgment”.

‘Spineless response’

However, in a post on X, Mr Polanski wrote: “I don’t think it would be ‘rushing to judgment’ to see that the press hounding people – especially people of colour – has been going on for a very long time.

“Really spineless response from the Prime Minister here that utterly fails to recognise the moment to tackle the press.”

On Sunday, Mr Polanski’s words escalated further. Responding to an article in the Mail on Sunday which praised this summer’s five heatwaves, he said: “It’s time we sorted out the press. Constant misinformation to protect their donors and fossil fuels is destroying lives and our planet. The Government must step up and stop being cowardly.”

He has also added his signature to a letter to the Prime Minister and Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, organised by the Good Law Project demanding an “immediate” public inquiry into the press.

It said: “There cannot be any doubt that Dr Arday’s tragic death was the direct, foreseeable and foreseen result of press harassment. A significant element in that harassment was the colour of his skin.

“The years since the Leveson inquiry have taught us that the press is not interested in self-regulation. Ipso has failed.

“We respectfully ask you to commission an immediate public inquiry into how to ensure a responsible press given its contribution to Dr Arday’s tragic death.”

He has also urged his supporters to sign a second petition calling for an inquiry into the “culture and behaviour” of the press, organised by Hacked Off, an organisation that has demanded state regulation of Fleet Street for the past 15 years.

The group has also urged ministers to push ahead with the second part of the Leveson inquiry into the culture and ethics of the press, which was launched in the wake of the phone hacking scandal at Rupert Murdoch’s newspaper empire.

Lord Young, founder of the Free Speech Union, told The Telegraph: “For the Green Party to pre-empt the inquest into [Mr Arday’s] death and weaponise it to pursue their anti-free speech agenda is both cynical and exploitative.

“The British press does not need to be ‘sorted out’. Scrutinising powerful and influential figures and holding them to account, including Zack Polanksi, is precisely what it should be doing.”

Kevin Hollinrake, chairman of the Conservative Party, said: “This is a straight up attack on free speech by the Green Party and once again proves that they are not serious about tackling the biggest issues facing our country.”

Earlier this month, Mr Polanski threw his support behind a petition to ban foreign media ownership as part of a “Media Sovereignty Act” in a speech at the Green Gathering Festival in Wales.

The petition calls for all members of the media to adhere to a statutory regulator and would force the sell-off of most national newspapers, including The Telegraph, which have foreign owners.

Mr Polanski told a panel at the festival: “Billionaires should not be able to have a monopoly on our free press. We need to push independent media like Byline Times, Novara Media [and] Turn Left.”

data.title: Zack Polanski may be a clown, but he’s also a threat to your freedom
data.description:
Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party, has been railing furiously against “misinformation”. And, for once, I have some sympathy with him. Misinformation is an appalling blight on our society.

To pick just one example, entirely at random. A Harley Street hypnotherapist once told a female client that, simply by harnessing the power of the unconscious mind, he could make her breasts grow bigger. Such a claim is, of course, preposterous. As I’m sure we can all agree, therefore, anyone capable of peddling such patent misinformation has no place in public life.

It so happens, however, that Polanski is not railing against “misinformation” in the field of boob enlargement. He’s referring solely to “misinformation” in newspapers. This week, he has demanded an inquiry into their “culture and behaviour”, while his Green Party colleagues have drawn up plans to give the state far-reaching powers over the press. Radical intervention, explains Polanski, is essential to stop newspapers “pushing constant misinformation”.

Naturally, I thank him for his input. I do, however, have one or two small questions. And so, at the risk of having the police set on me for daring to ask them, here they are.

First of all, what exactly is “misinformation”? And who should have the right to define it, on the entire country’s behalf?

I don’t know whether Polanski has considered the following possibility, but it’s not totally inconceivable that, at some point in the future, this country will have a Right-wing government. So how would he feel if that Right-wing government officially decided that it’s “misinformation” to say some women have penises, or that net zero is beneficial for the UK economy, or that Israel is guilty of genocide? Would Polanski be glad that the state had the authority to prevent newspapers from publishing claims of this kind?

This, I’m afraid, is the trouble with trying to tackle “misinformation”. It would be impossible to define it in a way everyone agreed with. Take Polanski himself. On Sunday, he ranted on social media that newspapers were “destroying lives and our planet” by publishing “constant misinformation to protect their donors and fossil fuels”. And what did he cite in evidence?

An opinion column from The Mail on Sunday, in which the writer confessed that he was actually rather enjoying this summer’s heatwaves. The writer did not deny that the heatwaves have caused serious problems – indeed, he listed many, from the wildfires to the disastrous impact on farmers’ crops. All the same, he felt that the rest of us should try to make the most of the hot weather, not least because it was bound to be cold and wet again soon.

That was it. Merely one writer’s personal view. Yet Polanski apparently deemed it to be “misinformation”, and thus unacceptable. Does this mean no columnist should be allowed to express a view of which he disapproves?

Oh, and if he’ll permit me to ask one more irritating question, does he think that, if the newspaper industry were under the thumb of the state, the public would ever have been allowed to know about the MPs’ expenses scandal? Of course, we can’t know for sure. But I think I can take a fairly good guess.

This is why, in my view, Polanski’s stated determination to “sort out” the press doesn’t only threaten the freedom of journalists, it also threatens the freedom of voters. In particular, those who dare to vote for parties of the Right. A Left-wing crackdown on the press will inevitably dictate what stories you’re allowed to know about, and what opinions you’re allowed to read. The Greens’ supposed war on “misinformation” will in reality prove to be a chillingly authoritarian war on conservative thought.

It’s clear, however, that beneath that imbecilic exterior lurks something that is not in the least comical. It is, on the contrary, darkly draconian. No matter how silly this gurning oddball may seem, therefore, we shouldn’t overlook the very real danger he would pose if he were to seize power in this country.

In light of which, I suppose I’d better watch what I say. So, just in case that fateful day ever dawns, allow me to place on record that I think Polanski is unsurpassably wise, spotlessly honourable and magnificently handsome. And that, furthermore, his foolproof plan to legalise crack cocaine will bring our nation nothing but joy.

There. Not a hint of misinformation in sight.

data.title: Monzo users hit by tech glitch
data.description:
Monzo suffered a major tech glitch which left thousands of customers facing problems with their banking app.

The online-only bank was forced to activate a backup service for customers after identifying problems with its main systems, which led to many services being curtailed. The issues were resolved several hours later.

At the time of the outage, Monzo warned that some app features might be unavailable and transactions could take longer, but said customers would still be able to make card payments, withdraw cash, and freeze their cards.

Monzo customers were also able to send and receive bank transfers on the backup service.

A spokesman for Monzo said: “For a short period today, we activated Monzo Stand-in, our fully independent backup bank while we investigated an issue affecting customers.

“This technical issue has been resolved, and all of our services are now back up and running. We’re sorry for any inconvenience and thank customers for their patience.”

Around 3,000 users reported problems with Monzo on Wednesday afternoon, according to DownDetector, which monitors tech issues on major websites and apps.

Monzo faced similar issues in January, when it also activated its so-called back-up bank after a tech problem.

It is the second major banking app glitch in two days after customers of Lloyds Bank, Halifax and Bank of Scotland were locked out of their online accounts on Tuesday.

They were left unable to transfer money, view online and app statements and pay for goods.

Monzo was founded in 2015 and now serves more than 10 million customers, making it the largest digital bank in the UK. It offers a range of current accounts and other investing services.

Gary Hoffman, the chairman, announced earlier this week that he would leave the fintech months after a shareholder revolt.

TS Anil, Monzo’s chief executive, also left in December last year following a dispute about Monzo’s strategy as it seeks to compete with Revolut, its much larger UK rival.

data.title: Italy is running out of Italians. A similar demographic catastrophe awaits Britain
data.description:
In the last couple of years I have been all over Italy. Mostly the south and the islands: Sardinia, Sicily, Puglia, Calabria – the periphery, the Mezzogiorno, the places where every travel writer is contractually obliged to note the picturesque decay alongside the antique dazzle.

And yes, I noted it. The crumbling palazzi, the feral verges, the towns half-shuttered by lunchtime. In the deep south you expect this. It is part of the deal, almost part of the charm. And Italy and Italians can still be wildly charming.

But in the last month I have been somewhere else. First the allegedly affluent north-east, around Trieste. Then, in the past week, I’ve been touring the wealthy industrial heartland south of Milan – the Po Valley, Pavia, Piacenza – the flatlands where Italy actually makes its manufacturing money.

And, I confess, I’ve been shocked. Because the chaos and decay of the south are now spreading right across Il Bel Paese.

The first thing you notice is the roads. Mamma Mia, are they bad. You can be driving on a main road between two proper towns and every hundred metres there is a pothole big enough to swallow a Fiat 500. Or so it feels. After a week of swerving, my nerves are shot and my axles are not much better. And my anxiety is based on hard fact. I checked.

In 2014 Rome half-abolished Italy’s provinces. It scrapped their elected governments, stripped their budgets – but left them owning 130,000 kilometres of road. Maintenance became a fiction. By 2017 provincial presidents were filing formal complaints with public prosecutors: legally covering themselves for the day the busted tarmac murdered someone. A year later, Genoa’s Morandi bridge fell into the Polcevera.

Last year the government announced a 70 per cent cut to provincial road funds, with Emilia-Romagna, the very region I’ve been rattling across, slated to lose half its money. Provincial chiefs warned that the only remaining option would be to close roads altogether.

Once you’ve noticed the dodgy roads, you start seeing everything else. The abandoned factories with their smashed skylights. The tatty, dying shopping centres. The graffiti almost everywhere.

This is what European decline looks like, and it has numbers attached.

Italy is the only major economy where real wages are lower than they were in 1990. GDP per head has barely budged since the euro arrived. Car production – in the land of Fiat, Alfa and Lancia – has collapsed to levels last seen in the 1950s.

Meanwhile, China has swallowed the textiles, shoes and furniture that once meant “Made in Italy” was an honourable boast.

And beneath it all is something starker: Italy is running out of Italians. Last year the country recorded 355,000 births – an all-time low and down nearly 40 per cent since 2008 – against 652,000 deaths. That is a natural loss of almost 300,000 people: a Verona, erased, annually. With a fertility rate of 1.14 and a median age of 49.1, Italy the oldest country in the EU.

What looks like decay may simply be what a very old country looks like – too few young workers to patch the tarmac, too few young families to fill the shops, too few taxpayers to pay for any of it.

We British love to tell ourselves we are uniquely doomed. We are not. In 1987 Italy celebrated “il sorpasso” – the moment its economy overtook ours. Nobody in Rome mentions il sorpasso now.

But before we get remotely superior, note the direction of travel: an ageing society, flatlining productivity, a state that cannot fix the basics. Italy may be the future of every Western nation that can’t make babies, and can’t compete with China.

I ended my latest Italian sojourn in a station bar full of young people in a little moonlit town near Piacenza. It was Sunday night. It was the World Cup final.

Italy, of course, was not playing. The Azzurri are now the first world champions in history to miss three consecutive World Cup tournaments. They have not kicked a ball at a finals since 2014, and this time they could not even qualify for a 48-team tournament.

The bar was, therefore, full of Italian kids who can barely remember their country competing at a World Cup. Yet they turned up anyway. And they dutifully watched other nations contest the final match – with a mixture of beery apathy and confected excitement.

Then at the whistle they said their ciaos and they pecked their kisses – and they silently dispersed, into the sultry darkness, down the winding, potholed roads.

data.title: Iran war hits small factories with £350,000 energy bill
data.description:
Small factories and swimming pools are among thousands of businesses facing a £350,000 energy shock from the Iran war, according to Cornwall Insight.

In new estimates, the energy consultant said that large leisure centres, including shopping centres and retail parks, have seen their energy bills rise by around 25pc since the conflict broke out in February.

For a site of that size, the increase would push their annual electricity bill up by around £128,000 to an average of £638,500. The same location could also expect its gas bill to jump by £230,000 to £1.15m.

This represents a combined increase of £358,000, with costs likely to be passed on to households.

The energy shock risks piling more pressure on the economy by reviving inflation fears, dampening the Prime Minister’s hopes of tackling the cost of living.

The situation also risks worsening as the war drags on. The price of oil was back up to $93 a barrel on Thursday amid the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

As well as the war’s effect on prices, Cornwall Insight also cited net zero transition costs as a driver for higher bills.

Jacob Briggs, of Cornwall Insight, said: “On top of rising wholesale prices, businesses are also seeing increases in other parts of the bill to pay for network upgrades and balancing costs.

“While these are necessary to support the energy transition, unlike households, the cost support that’s available is highly targeted so a lot of businesses will struggle with the rises.”

Sir Keir Starmer’s government announced relief on some costs for the most energy-intensive businesses while Andy Burnham has said he will remove the 5pc VAT charged on households’ electricity bills this winter.

The warning on rising bills came as a growing share of manufacturers reported plans to raise prices in the coming months.

A survey from the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) found 30pc of factory bosses expected to raise prices in the coming quarter, with just 8pc set to cut costs for customers.

Cameron Martin, an economist at the CBI, urged Mr Burnham and John Healey, the Chancellor, to avoid adding more costs in October’s Budget.

“Instead, the Government should use the Budget to build on efforts to restore competitiveness – delivering the British industrial competitiveness scheme while going further to support reindustrialisation by reducing policy-driven energy costs for all businesses,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Food and Drink Federation said 88pc of companies reported a deterioration in business conditions since Labour came to power in 2024.

This has already pushed a number of high-profile companies to the brink.

Harvey Nichols nearly became the latest victim before Frasers Group bought the department store out of administration for £40m.

Frasers announced on Thursday that it had offered “goodwill payments” to a number of personal shoppers and stylists who were owed money after Harvey Nichols’s collapse.

A spokesman for the company said: “Where possible, Frasers Group does its best to be supportive of individual traders and small businesses.”

A government spokesman said: “Businesses will continue to pay the price if the UK is dependent on fossil fuel markets that we do not control. Bringing bills down for good is our priority and clean power is key to how we get there.”

data.title: London taxi drivers risk black cab shortage
data.description:
London taxi drivers face the threat of a black cab shortage after a Chinese manufacturer radically scaled back production.

Drivers and fleet operators in the capital have complained of nine-month waiting times for even small numbers of cars from the London Electric Vehicle Company (LEVC), which is currently the sole manufacturer available.

Dwindling demand for black cabs means the Coventry-based group, owned by Chinese giant Geely, has cut production of the celebrated vehicles as the popularity of ride-hailing apps lead to fewer drivers.

But its “build-to-order” policy has been blamed for creating a shortfall of electric taxis, just as net zero rules imposed by Transport for London (TfL) force drivers to retire their older diesel vehicles and buy new ones.

At the moment, mainstream manufacturers such as Ford, Stellantis and Nissan do not produce a London taxi because it would not be financially viable, leaving LEVC’s electric TX cab as the only option.

Mick Walker, the secretary of the London Cab Drivers Club, said: “Everyone is starting to realise the trade is in serious trouble.

“There are drivers being put out of work now because they cannot actually get a vehicle.”

Steve McNamara, the general secretary of the Licenced Taxi Drivers’ Association, stressed that the secondhand market for black cabs remained healthy, giving individuals an alternative option.

But he warned that things were particularly tough for fleet operators that only buy new.

Colts Cabs, London’s largest fleet operator with more than 1,000 cabs, typically replaces between 100 and 200 vehicles per year but said it had been offered just 10 cars when it attempted to order 30 in March.

Mr McNamara said: “Fleets are really struggling to get hold of new vehicles.

“In recent weeks and months, there have been attempts to place orders for 200 cabs and people are being told they can only have 25 and not until February next year at the earliest.”

An LEVC spokesman said the company “regularly adjusts manufacturing output to meet expected market demand” but insisted that the cuts to production were also the result of work to gear up for the launch of a new model.

He added: “In the meantime, TX assembly continues and new vehicle deliveries, used sales and aftersales operations continue as normal.”

The most recently available accounts published by the company say it produced 1,308 cars in 2024, or about 25 per week. However, the figure is thought to have fallen since then.

China’s Geely acquired the London Taxi Company, now known as LEVC, in 2013.

The automotive giant, which also owns Lotus, Volvo and Polestar, later invested £500m in a cutting-edge factory in Ansty Business Park on the outskirts of Coventry.

Its business plan assumed demand for its world-famous taxis from London and other world cities, with a van variant also developed as a sideline.

However, industry sources say demand in both categories has been disappointing globally.

In particular, LEVC says it has cut production in response to a dramatic decline in the number of licenced taxi drivers in London.

Since 2020, the figure has plunged from about 20,400 to 15,900.

However, cabbies argue that the company’s “build-to-order” policy is failing to keep pace with demand for replacement vehicles, creating a vicious feedback loop where cars become even less affordable and more drivers are squeezed out.

Under TfL rules related to air quality, black cabs must be retired after 12 years.

The policy will mean some 1,300 cars are taken off the streets in the next 11 months alone, according to the London Cab Drivers Club.

At the same time, rising input costs and high interest rates have pushed up the cost of LEVC’s electric taxis.

When the TX was introduced in 2018, the base purchase price stood at under £55,000. It has since increased to more than £74,000 – with cabbies who cannot afford this upfront cost typically paying more than £90,000 when financing deals are taken into account.

LEVC has blamed this rising cost of ownership for falling demand, as well as the shrinking number of drivers taking “The Knowledge” test and entering the trade.

Whereas some 3,400 people applied in 2000, only 809 people did so last year – with only 107 passing.

Mr Walker blamed the drop on the ease with which drivers can now qualify instead as a private hire operator and then ply London for work on apps such as Uber and Bolt.

Whereas it typically takes three to four years to memorise the hundreds of routes they could be tested on, he said, a private hire driver can obtain a licence in just three to four weeks.

“There’s no one coming into the trade, really,” he warned, pointing to figures showing that last week just one black-cab driver qualified compared to more than 600 private hire drivers.

There are some 109,700 private hire drivers in London overall.

A TfL spokesman said: “London’s taxis play a vital role in keeping the capital moving, and we continue to work closely with the taxi trade and vehicle manufacturers. 

“It’s important that London continues to have enough licensed taxis to meet customer demand and that drivers can access vehicles that meet the standards required to operate in the capital.”

The spokesman added: “We’ll continue to engage closely with LEVC and representatives of the taxi trade, while monitoring the situation closely.”

data.title: UK’s biggest banks warn Burnham against ‘damaging’ windfall tax
data.description:
Britain’s biggest banks have warned Andy Burnham against introducing a “damaging” windfall tax on the UK’s finance industry.

In a letter on Thursday, lobby group UK Finance warned the Government that increasing the current levies placed on the sector would threaten to undermine Mr Burnham’s plan to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

There is fresh speculation that John Healey, the Chancellor, could launch a fresh raid on bank profits in his maiden Budget on Oct 28.

However, UK Finance said it was “concerned that increasing taxes on banks would ultimately risk undermining the very tax base the Government seeks to protect and grow, as well as damaging the UK’s international competitiveness”.

The letter added: “While fully recognising the fiscal pressures facing the Government, raising what are already high sector-specific taxes would run counter to the wider growth agenda.”

The warning follows calls from the Green Party for a new 38pc windfall tax on all bank profits more than £800m.

The policy is aimed at raising £19bn for the Treasury to lower National Insurance costs for small businesses.

It emerged earlier this week that Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, had warned Mr Healey that raising taxes on UK banks could trigger staff to move abroad.

Mr Dimon reportedly told Mr Healey that higher taxes in London had contributed to jobs moving away from the city.

Sir Howard Davies, the former chairman of NatWest, has also cautioned Mr Burnham against the move, telling The Telegraph last week that new bank taxes risked sending banking activities abroad.

British banks already pay one of the highest tax rates in the world at nearly 47pc, according to UK Finance.

In Amsterdam, the rate is 42pc, while Frankfurt charges 39pc and New York charges 28pc.

The taxes include a 3pc corporation tax surcharge on profits of more than £100m, plus a levy on the value of their assets.

Germany is planning to lower corporation tax by 1pc each year between 2028 and 2032, which could make Frankfurt more attractive, the letter says.

Banking accounts for more than £1 out of every £25 of the UK’s economic output, UK Finance claimed.

It added: “At a time when peer jurisdictions are seeking to improve their competitiveness, it is vital that the UK’s approach to both tax and regulation pull in the same direction, supporting investment and the sector’s capacity to finance growth across the economy.”

data.title: One in eight Britons to take weight loss drugs by 2027
data.description:
One in eight Britons will be taking weight loss drugs by 2027, a new report has predicted.

The number of UK adults taking glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) weight loss medication will more than double from three million to seven million by next year, according to analysis by consulting firm PwC Strategy&, accounting for 13pc of the population.

This uptick will be fuelled by the approval of a new Wegovy pill, which will make weight loss treatment easier and more accessible.

This is expected to trigger a sharp drop in the sale of sweets and crisps, according to PwC, as the rollout dramatically changes consumer spending patterns.

Those already taking the medication cut their spending on snacks and sweet treats by 70pc and spent 60pc less on sugary drinks, PwC Strategy& found in a survey of more than 2,300 adults.

The latest findings have been released just weeks after the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved a tablet version of the blockbuster weight loss drug Wegovy.

This is the UK’s first GLP-1 pill for weight loss and can now be prescribed to adults with obesity.

It means that millions of Britons can access GLP-1 drugs, which mimic gut hormones to regulate people’s appetites, without needing to administer them by a weekly injection.

The pills will soon be rolled out across major retailers including Boots, Morrisons and Superdrug.

However, they are not yet available on the NHS. Before this can happen, the pill will need to be evaluated by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

While businesses selling confectionery or fast food will suffer from a drop-off in spending on unhealthy foods, those selling healthy products are likely to see a surge in sales.

GLP-1 users spent 60pc more on fresh food, 54pc more on high-protein options and 40pc more on vitamins and supplements, PwC Strategy& found.

They also spent 30pc more on fitness and an additional 40pc on clothing.

These spending patterns are likely to continue even after they have lost weight and stopped taking the drugs.

More than 80pc of those who had stopped treatment said they maintained at least some of the dietary changes they had made while taking the GLP-1s.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK, said: “GLP-1 is the most consumerised medication today. Who your GLP-1 customers are, and how your category changes, will dictate how brands and retailers compete.

“We’ll see consumer businesses reshape their portfolios to manage near-term risk.”

More than a quarter (28pc) of GLP-1 users said they would maintain their current levels of spending on the drugs even if the cost of living rose.

The drugs, which are only prescribed on the NHS for those with severe obesity, have predominantly been purchased by wealthier households, but are becoming increasingly mainstream.

Of current users, 6pc came from lower-income households, compared to 20pc for wealthier households.

Adoption of weight loss drugs has so far been highest among women, who account for 60pc of current users.

data.title: Taxpayers cover £110m cladding bill for hedge fund-owned housebuilder
data.description:
A housebuilder controlled by a major Wall Street hedge fund has secured taxpayer funding to remove potentially dangerous cladding from its buildings.

Avant Homes, which is owned by US investor Elliott Management, has agreed a “payment plan” with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government to help meet a potential £113m bill for critical safety works.

The deal transfers responsibility from Avant to the state for carrying out remediation works after the Grenfell Tower tragedy in 2017. Since 2020, housebuilders have been expected to arrange and pay for this repair work themselves.

But in accounts filed to Companies House, Avant said it was “no longer required to undertake or procure works” on buildings that needed their cladding replaced. Instead, building work would be paid for “via a government funded scheme”, allowing it to defer repayment.

Under the plan, Avant is expected to fully repay the costs with interest “over a number of years”, according to filings. The terms were kept confidential.

Avant’s latest accounts contain a £113m provision for safety repairs, reflecting rules brought in after the Grenfell fire.

The disaster, which killed 72 people, resulted in laws holding developers responsible for remediation work dating back 30 years.

Avant, which is chaired by Jeff Fairburn, the former Persimmon boss, said its new agreement provided crucial “liquidity support” as it sought to secure a new debt facility before a deadline of Oct 31.

It said it was in “advanced discussions” about the refinancing.

Avant’s latest accounts warned it was facing financial pressures that cast doubt on its ability to continue as a going concern. Pre-tax losses exceeded £111m in the year ending June 2025, while its finance costs stood at £93.3m.

Net liabilities surged to £160.4m, up from £48.9m in the previous year, in part driven by remediation works.

Avant is owned by one of the world’s largest hedge funds, Elliott Management, which manages around $80bn (£59bn) in assets globally.

The housebuilder has previously argued that the tower blocks in question were constructed under its previous owner, before new cladding rules were brought in.

A spokesman for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We have agreed a payment plan with Avant, giving the company longer to repay debt owed to the Government under the developer remediation contract including interest, which safeguards taxpayers’ money.

“We will continue to work to speed up cladding removal and bring the building safety crisis to an end.”

Mr Fairburn previously left FTSE 100 housebuilder Persimmon after receiving an £82m bonus in 2018.

The payment prompted widespread criticism from shareholders and MPs, since Persimmon had benefited substantially from the taxpayer-backed Help to Buy scheme.

Avant and Elliott Management were contacted for comment.

data.title: Sick of yobs blasting out music on the bus? Here’s my simple solution
data.description:
What do you think would be an appropriate punishment for young men who blast out music from their phones on public transport? Death by firing squad? Hanging, drawing and quartering? Or are you one of those bleeding-heart pinko liberals who think a whole-life sentence in Belmarsh would suffice?

Well, whatever your answer, it may be time to think again. Because, according to a top academic, we should show these unfairly maligned youths more understanding.

Prof Orla Muldoon, the head of the School of Psychology at Queen’s University Belfast, has told the BBC that such people aren’t necessarily being antisocial. Quite the opposite, in fact. She says: “It is quintessentially social to play music, and hope your peers appreciate that music.”

Yes, that must be it. These misunderstood young gentlemen merely wish us to share in their passion for great art. When some 19-year-old Neet sees the careworn faces of his fellow train or bus passengers, he thinks: “These poor commuters. They all look so miserable. And no wonder. It must be awful, having to work for a living. Still, I know what will cheer them up. Being forced to listen at ear-splitting volume to a blisteringly obnoxious drill rap track in which a small-time drug-dealer boasts of stabbing a schoolboy to death for looking at him funny in the queue for fried chicken.”

For me, though, the real question is not why these yobs behave like this. It’s why they all seem to have the exact same taste in music. Always hip-hop. Never any other genre. In my many years of commuting, I for one have yet to encounter anyone using their phone to blast out Classic FM, or BBC Radio 3.

“Excuse me, young man, but would you mind plugging in some headphones? I can’t stand Schubert.”

“What’s your problem, bruv? You not appreciate a good symphony in B-flat major? You got something against song cycles about alienation and solitude in early 19th-century Prussia?”

Come to think of it, that gives me an idea. Next time I find myself on a train near someone who’s inflicting his music on everyone in earshot, I’m going to give him a taste of his own medicine – by drowning out his music with mine. And make it a type of music he’s liable to dislike, such as opera or Baroque – just to see what he says in response. “Hey, bossman, gonna turn that racket down? It’s well inconsiderate. I can hardly hear a note of my industrial horrorcore.”

Of course, there is a risk he’ll turn violent. But I’m not too worried. The writer Theodore Dalrymple used to be a prison doctor. And in his latest book, he says that a prison officer he once worked with noticed an intriguing pattern. When the inmates were allowed to listen to hip-hop, they would often become agitated, and start fighting. Yet when they were made to listen to classical music, “they calmed down and became more tractable”.

So, with luck, I’ll only be beaten up very gently.

A quick question for the trans mob

Over in the US, the row about transgender ideology has just taken an unexpected new turn. It began when a female basketball star named Gabby Williams declared that trans women (i.e. biological males) would be “welcome” to play for her team. Unfortunately, her efforts to be inclusive appear to have backfired. Because not one but two male former basketball stars have suddenly claimed that they now identify as women – in what looks suspiciously like a crafty ploy to show how silly the whole business is.

Former New York Knicks player Enes Kanter Freedom – who is 6ft 10in tall – said: “If simply declaring who you are is all that’s required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA [Women’s National Basketball Association].” Meanwhile, former Sacramento Kings player Royce White – who is 6ft 8in – said he merely wants “a fair chance to participate as a sometimes-identifying-as-a-transgender-woman athlete”.

data.title: Thames Water issues warning over reservoir levels
data.description:
Thames Water has told customers to take shorter showers after warning that reservoir levels are lower than usual amid the drought.

The utility, which has 16 million customers, said its London reservoirs were 74pc full at the end of last month. That is below the average 87pc level where it usually sits at this time of year.

Its Farmoor Reservoir in Oxfordshire was 92pc full, though this too was below average and the company said the water level there was declining. Between 1989 and 2019, Farmoor was typically 96.4pc full at the end of July.

Thames said it was important that customers continued to follow a hosepipe ban introduced on July 23 and urged people to cut water usage in other ways.

Martin Padley, at Thames Water, said: “With reservoir levels below where we would expect them to be for this time of year, and demand remaining high, we’re asking customers to keep going and continue using only what they need.

“Small changes, such as taking shorter showers, turning off taps and avoiding non-essential water use outdoors, all help reduce pressure on our network while our teams continue working around the clock to find and fix leaks.”

Weeks without rain have left 71.3pc of England in drought. Heatwaves have also led to increased demand for water. Thames said customers across London and the Thames Valley used around 100 million litres more water than normal each day during July’s hot weather.

Experts have warned that despite rain being forecast in the next few days, it will take many weeks before reservoir levels return to normal.

Thames Water said rainfall has been around 40pc of the long-term average since March.

The exceptionally dry spring and summer have led to concern that further restrictions may be needed. While millions of households across England already face hosepipe bans, businesses could face restrictions if dry weather persists.

Under the next stage of its emergency drought plans, Thames Water could ask ministers to authorise restrictions on car washes, window washing and private swimming pools, including in gyms if it becomes necessary.

Water bans becoming more common

Southern Water became the first utility to apply for a Drought Order and a Non-Essential Use Ban in the Isle of Wight and Hampshire.

Anglian Water, which supplies seven million customers mostly in the East of England, has also warned it would consider such a ban if supplies fall further.

The hosepipe ban has so far reduced demand by 3pc in London and 6pc across the Thames Valley and the Home Counties.

As well as making Britons thirstier and prompting them to have more showers, the dry and hot weather is putting greater pressure on water pipes deep in the ground.

Thames’s ageing network of pipes are at risk of cracking as London’s dry clay soil hardens and leads to hairline fractures in the pipes. It is fixing more than 1,000 leaks every week, a fifth more than normal.

Some 27 million people across England are under hosepipe bans. Wessex Water announced its first ban in 50 years on Monday, affecting families in Bath, Somerset, Dorset and Wiltshire.

The boss of the utility said the dry weather meant water demand had been 30pc above average for this time of year, “the equivalent of almost half a million hosepipes running for a full hour every day”.

Andy Burnham last week chaired a Cobra meeting on extreme heat, wildfires and drought. The Prime Minister said Britain had to “face up to the changing climate”.

Proposals have been put forward to allow water companies to charge “surge” prices during times of drought to push people to use less. However, the Prime Minister has signalled he will intervene to drop the plan, which is currently under consideration by regulator Ofwat.

data.title: Disney sues Trump administration in free speech row
data.description:
Disney has sued the Trump administration in an escalating row between the White House and the media over free speech.

The media giant and its ABC division have filed a lawsuit accusing Donald Trump’s media regulator of waging a “retaliatory campaign” against the broadcaster because it disagrees with its output.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ordered Disney in April to begin the renewal process for its television broadcast licences ahead of schedule.

The watchdog has also opened an investigation into The View, an ABC talk show, while officials have been carrying out a long-running review of diversity, equity and inclusion policies at Disney.

In the lawsuit, Disney urged a judge to block the early licence renewal, which it described as an attack on the freedom of the press.

Lawyers for the company accused the FCC of attempting to retaliate against a network that “⁠refuses to bow to the administration’s demands”.

Disney separately filed for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, accusing the FCC of an “extraordinary assault on free speech”.

In its lawsuit, Disney alleged the Trump administration was trying to intimidate the rest of US media industry.

“ABC is the visible target and suffers the most immediate harm, but the message is addressed to every broadcaster in the country, and the ultimate cost is borne by the press as a whole,” according to the lawsuit.

It marks the latest escalation in a long-running clash between media groups and the Trump administration over the White House’s attempts to tame the press.

Mr Trump has previously sued major US broadcasters, including ABC, for defamation, securing millions of dollars in settlements.

However, news groups have increasingly fought back. Last year, NPR sued the US government arguing its funding cuts had hit its First Amendment rights.

The BBC has also chosen to fight a defamation lawsuit brought by the Mr Trump over an episode of Panorama, demanding personal documents and financial records from the US president.

The row with Disney comes as Mr Trump grapples with falling poll ratings ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The US president has repeatedly criticised Disney’s ABC network, accusing the network of bias in favour of the Democrats.

The FCC, which is led by Trump ally Brendan Carr, has in turn stepped up pressure on the company, suggesting it could be engaged in “illegal DEI discrimination”.

The row came to a head last year after late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel accused Mr Trump and his supporters of trying to capitalise on the killing of Right-wing influencer Charlie Kirk.

Mr Kimmel was briefly pulled from the air amid a backlash from Republicans, but was reinstated a few days later.

The pair clashed again in April this year after Mr Kimmel joked that Melania Trump, the first lady, had a “glow like an expectant widow”.

The comments came days before the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner was abandoned after a gunman attempted to storm the room. Mr Trump claimed that Mr Kimmel’s comments were a “despicable call to violence”. Mr Kimmel said it was a “very light” joke about the age difference between the president and his wife.

Disney’s ABC network owns and operates eight regional TV stations in cities including Los Angeles, New York and San Francisco.

Broadcast licences are usually renewed every eight years and Disney’s were reportedly not up for renewal until 2028.

An FCC spokesman said: “All broadcasters have a legal obligation to operate in the public interest – even Disney.”

He added: “The FCC will continue to follow the facts and law wherever they lead.”

data.title: Barclays faces legal fight with investors over ex-boss’s Epstein links
data.description:
Barclays faces a legal fight with investors over claims they were misled about Jes Staley’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein.

The British banking giant risks being sued for hundreds of millions of pounds in the High Court, in the first UK claim triggered by the actions of its former chief executive.

The investors, who are being represented by City litigation fund Woodsford, claim to have suffered vast stock market losses when the truth about Mr Staley’s ties to Epstein came to light.

Mr Staley was close friends with Epstein and even visited him in Florida in 2009 while he was serving his prison sentence for procuring a minor for prostitution.

He had first met Epstein in 1999 while head of JP Morgan’s private banking division.

However, it is claimed that Barclays failed to disclose the true extent of Mr Staley’s relationship with Epstein to investors for the entirety of his tenure as the bank’s chief executive.

Mr Staley, who ran Barclays between 2015 and 2021, was later issued with a £1.1m fine and a lifetime ban from the City over his relationship with the disgraced paedophile financier.

This came after Mr Staley was found to have misled Barclays about the nature of his relationship with Epstein and the point of their last contact.

The misinformation led to Barclays writing to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to deny that Mr Staley had a close relationship with Epstein in the wake of the paedophile financier’s death in August 2019.

Thousands of emails subsequently revealed that Mr Staley had described Epstein as one of his “deepest” and “most cherished” friends.

In the same year he was appointed Barclays chief executive, Mr Staley made two visits to Epstein’s properties in the US Virgin Islands, court documents stated.

Mr Staley also used his own daughter as an intermediary to communicate with Epstein after becoming Barclays’ boss.

Investors are preparing to sue Barclays on the basis they were deceived over Mr Staley’s Epstein ties, which led to them suffering large losses when revelations came to light.

In particular, they claim to have suffered losses when Barclays’ share price fell on three separate occasions between 2021 and 2023.

That includes Nov 1, 2021, when Mr Staley resigned from Barclays, and on Mar 9, 2023 when JP Morgan filed a complaint against him in relation to his alleged knowledge of Epstein’s exploitation of women.

The final so-called stock drop occurred on Oct 12, 2023 when the FCA issued Mr Staley with its lifetime ban.

Mr Staley has repeatedly denied that he had a close friendship with Epstein and previously unsuccessfully challenged the FCA’s lifetime ban. After the decision was upheld last year, he reiterated that he was “never dishonest”.

Barclays allegedly omitted information from reports

Woodsford claims that investors’ collective losses across those three dates amount to £2bn.

Lawyers instructed by a group of investors claim Barclays breached its obligations by failing to disclose risks posed by Mr Staley’s Epstein ties.

These include allegations that Barclays omitted information from its 2019 and 2020 annual reports despite claims it hired a law firm to review thousands of emails which appeared to depict a close relationship between the two men.

The proposed claim echoes a similar lawsuit filed against Barclays in the US, where the bank has been accused of “material misrepresentations over the status and nature of Staley’s relationship with Epstein”.

Legal documents filed in the US claim that “when defendants’ deception of the FCA and investors was revealed, the price of Barclays fell and investors were economically damaged”.

Woodsford has said that it will sue Barclays if a settlement is not reached.

Barclays was contacted for comment.

data.title: Taxpayer-owned British Steel owes China £1bn
data.description:
Taxpayer-owned British Steel owed almost £1bn to its former Chinese owners when it was nationalised by Labour, newly published accounts showed.

The Government formally took ownership of the struggling business last month in a move aimed at protecting jobs and keeping the blast furnaces going at its site in Scunthorpe, Lincolnshire.

But recent accounts reveal the scale of liabilities taxpayers face as a result, including substantial debts owed by the loss-making company alongside ongoing operational costs.

These include at least £960m that British Steel owed to Jingye, its former Chinese parent, in the form of intercompany loans at the end of 2024.

Jingye is expected to pursue that sum as compensation and has already begun proceedings under an existing UK-China investment treaty.

The accounts also suggest that simply keeping British Steel afloat will be a costly endeavour in itself.

The document, signed off by Jingye just days before the company was nationalised, says a fresh funding injection of “£275m to £330m” will be needed “over the next 12 months” alone. The Treasury has already provided some £555m of working capital to the business.

At the same time, British Steel’s physical assets – including property, plant and equipment – have been deemed largely worthless after an audit review.

The company, which employs 2,700 workers, cannot produce steel profitably. British Steel reported sales of £829m in 2024, but made a loss of £254m. This was equivalent to a loss of £201 per tonne of steel, before taxes, the accounts said.

Liquid steel production also fell by nearly a quarter to 1.3 million tonnes after the business suffered “severe and persistent operational problems” in 2024.

These included periods where only one furnace was available, as well as several “chill” events, where blast furnaces failed to sustain the heat required for production.

The furnaces were so unstable that on several occasions steel was deemed too poor quality to be used, the documents said.

One industry source likened the company to a “money pit”, adding: “The longer they keep the blast furnaces open, the longer they are going to lose money hand over fist.

“Obviously, closure is pretty unpalatable from a political point of view though. It’s also hard to imagine anyone being very happy about giving money to Jingye.”

The Government first seized operational control of British Steel in April 2025 from ‌Jingye after ministers became concerned that the Chinese company was seeking to irreversibly close the blast furnaces.

This was primarily based on a belief that the company was failing to buy enough raw materials to keep them going – a claim that Jingye denies.

Parliament later passed a bill that allowed ministers to take formal ownership of the plant in the public interest, which took effect in July this year.

That bill also required the Government to consider what compensation, if any, was payable to Jingye.

It is understood that this process, which will begin in the autumn and be overseen by an independent valuer, could determine that no money is ultimately due.

The decision by the former Starmer premiership to nationalise the company triggered a backlash from Beijing, which said it was “strongly dissatisfied” at the time.

A government spokesman said on Thursday: “After assessing the impact on our economy, critical national infrastructure and national security, we concluded that public ownership was the best way to secure British Steel’s future and protect the future of UK steel production.

“An independent valuer would determine what, if any, is payable to Jingye, and our focus is now on stabilising the business, backing the communities that rely on it and building a sustainable, competitive and decarbonised steel sector for the years ahead.”

data.title: Raleigh’s downfall is an indictment of British manufacturing
data.description:
With famous models such as the Grifter, the Burner and, perhaps most of all, the Chopper, Raleigh remains one of the most treasured brands in cycling history.

Older readers will recall the latter fondly as one of the most wished-for Christmas gifts of the 1970s.

And yet this week we learned that Accell, the Dutch owner of the bike manufacturer, has filed for insolvency.

Sure, companies run into trouble all the time. And yet, the long and painful decline of Raleigh is surely emblematic of everything that has gone wrong with British manufacturing in the last 50 years – and unfortunately there is not much point in talking about building new industries if we can’t keep the old ones alive.

In some parallel universe, Raleigh might be a huge success. After all, it is not as if cycling isn’t popular.

Indeed, in most British cities you can hardly cross the street without a few bikers whizzing past you. Around 17pc of us cycle regularly, while in countries such as the Netherlands it is more than 50pc.

The global market is worth an estimated $35bn (£26bn), and it is growing at 6pc-plus every year. Put simply, this is an industry where there is plenty of money to be made.

And yet, to put it mildly, none of that has helped Raleigh.

Traced back to a small Nottingham workshop in 1885, the company grew into the world’s largest bicycle maker by 1913, retaining that crown for decades. It was synonymous with reliable, simple transport and one of the major employers in the East Midlands.

In the past 50 years, however, it has been a sad tale of relentless decline. It was taken over by the largely forgotten industrial conglomerate Tube Investments (TI), before falling into the hands of the German-owned Derby Cycles, and finally that of Accell from the Netherlands.

Production here in Britain ended more than 20 years ago, and now its latest owner has filed for insolvency.

Perhaps someone else will buy out the branding rights from the administrators. Or perhaps they won’t.

We will find out in the next few weeks, but whatever happens, it is hard to see Raleigh surviving as anything more than a badge – and perhaps not even that.

This keeps happening. Denby Pottery, another brand with a great heritage, appointed administrators earlier this year, and stopped production after 200 years.

Liberty Steel has closed, and most of what remains of the industry has been nationalised.

It is hard to believe that Jaguar Land Rover will be with us much longer, given how many mistakes the company has made, or its enthusiasm for trashing a brand that was once one of the best in the global market for upmarket cars. The list goes on.

All the major developed economies struggle to stay competitive in manufacturing, given the rise of first Japanese and now Chinese rivals. But Britain struggles more than most.

There is no other major country that has lost so many key industries so completely as we have. The result?

We have already dropped out of the top 10 global manufacturing nations, overtaken by the likes of Mexico and even Russia, and we show little sign of recovering our place among the world’s leaders any time soon.

We need to learn the lessons of that. The UK has been for too long a brutal place to run a manufacturing business.

It started with the trade union militancy of the 1960s and 1970s, which made it harder and harder for the likes of Raleigh to remain competitive, first with the rest of Europe and then with Asia.

The industrial conglomerates of the 1980s may have briefly stopped some of the rot, but conglomerates such as TI, or rivals such as Hanson and BTR, lacked the expertise or ambition to grow the brands they controlled – and have since mostly disappeared.

As this century has unfolded, it has become even worse, with punishingly high energy prices and green levies that could have been purposely designed to make it as hard as possible to produce anything in a factory. It has been a long downward trend, with only brief pauses on the way.

The new Government led by Andy Burnham talks a lot about reviving manufacturing and creating new industries. But what is the point if we can’t keep the ones we already have alive?

There is not much hope of dominating solar power or microchips or space launchers – or whatever the latest Business Secretary has decided will generate the right kind of headlines this week – if we can’t make a bike. We are just kidding ourselves. It is not going to happen.

It doesn’t have to be impossible. We need far lower corporate taxes; much cheaper industrial energy; more flexible labour rules; an end to planning restrictions that make it virtually impossible to expand plants in the right place; better infrastructure; trade deals that allow access to the biggest markets on fair terms; and welfare reforms that make it possible to find people to do the jobs that are needed if a business happens to start growing again.

There is nothing very complicated about it. With the right mix, more companies would survive and might actually start growing again.

But right now there is very little sign that the new Government, for all its rhetoric about helping the North – or actually the East Midlands in this case – understands what is needed any more than the last few did.

There are probably plenty of teenagers, who already have vinyl collections and VHS players, who would like to find a retro Chopper under the Christmas tree, and parents who would pay handsomely for it, especially if it had the authenticity of being “Made in Nottingham”.

But it is not going to happen. Raleigh’s long decline is a sorry tale of industrial incompetence, and unfortunately it looks as if there is little sign of that ending any time soon.

data.title: Vistry shares dive as Allianz cuts insurance cover for suppliers
data.description:
Vistry shares dived nearly 10pc after a major credit insurer cut its cover for suppliers to the housebuilder.

The company fell sharply on Monday after reports that Allianz Trade warned suppliers in recent weeks that it was changing its credit limits for Vistry, which could lead to cover being cut by up to 70pc.

The housebuilder’s stock fell by around 9pc during early trading.

The credit squeeze, first reported by the Financial Times, could mean that Vistry faces another squeeze on its cash flow. Under Adam Daniels, its new chief executive, the housebuilder has already resorted to aggressive discounting and slowing down construction to produce more cash to pay down its debt.

Anthony Codling, from RBC Capital Markets, said the market’s reaction “suggests that investors are concerned about the potential impacts on Vistry’s cash flow and the size and scale of its business going forward”.

He said: “If a supplier cannot secure credit insurance and it is worried about getting paid, it is likely to request payment upfront from its customers.

“In Vistry’s case, this would put more pressure on its already-strapped cash flow by having to make payments upfront or it may lead to it building fewer homes if it cannot secure the materials it needs to build more homes.”

A spokesman for Vistry said: “We are not aware of any supplier withdrawing trade from Vistry due to credit insurance changes and we have seen no interruptions to our supply chain.

“Credit insurers continue to provide substantial cover for our supply chain which more than meets the group’s requirements on an ongoing basis.

“We remain confident in our ability to deliver a substantial reduction in average net debt levels in the second half of 2026 and continue to forecast a net cash position in excess of £100m at the end of 2026.”

Shares in Vistry have dropped by more than 80pc since August 2024, when it reached a high of close to £14.

The decline comes after an earnings call last week in which Duncan Cooper, the chief financial officer of Travis Perkins, a building supplies company, flagged that credit insurance was being “pulled” from a “fairly significant national housebuilder” as a yardstick for how much pressure the construction industry is under.

He told analysts: “Got a phone call on Friday to say ... a final element of credit insurance had been pulled on a fairly significant national housebuilder.

“These are things we have to take into account and be considerate to. The stress is real.”

Sources told the Financial Times that Mr Cooper was referring to Vistry.

A spokesman for Travis Perkins said: “As a matter of principle, Travis Perkins does not comment on individual customers.”

Housebuilders across the board have been hit by rising build costs, persistently high mortgage rates and regulatory constraints, which have led to a slump in construction activity.

Allianz Trade declined to comment.

data.title: TfL ‘understated’ fare-dodging bill by £20m
data.description:
Transport for London (TfL) could be understating the cost of fare dodging by more than £20m after officials admitted to curbing their estimates.

The transport group estimated that fare evasion across the Underground network cost about £190m last year.

But TfL officials told Tube Alerter, a website that tracks travel disruptions, that it applied a 10pc reduction to the amount lost to evaders because it had no way to accurately measure evasion across the network.

This has not been included in its estimated total, meaning the true cost of fare evasion for TfL is potentially £21m higher at £211m.

This far exceeds the £168m of extra revenue TfL hopes to raise this year by increasing fares across its entire bus, Underground and Overground network.

In its disclosure, officials said the reduction reflected a “medium confidence” level in its data.

Under TfL’s approach to fare-dodging, its enforcement teams target hotspots where evasion is most rampant, meaning that the data may not reflect patterns across the wider network.

TfL has reportedly cited the lack of an automated system that is capable of cross-referencing each passenger journey with a corresponding payment for its patchy figures.

The figures have drawn sharp criticism from the opposition at City Hall.

Thomas Turrell, a transport spokesman for the City Hall Conservatives, accused Sir Sadiq Khan of having “lost control of fare evasion”.

He said Sir Sadiq had allowed TfL to become trapped in a “doom loop”, where underestimating the data led to underestimation of the problem.

A TfL spokesman said: “Robust analysis of fare evasion on London’s transport network is a vital tool in tackling it, and the estimated total cost of fare evasion is just one of many figures we produce to measure the scale of the issue.

“All figures produced are estimates that are calculated according to TfL’s best interpretation of the data, in line with industry standards.

“The estimated cost of £190m represents an evidence-based assessment that takes limitations of the data used into account.”

data.title: Hollywood billionaire Ellison pledges to make more British TV
data.description:
Hollywood billionaire David Ellison has pledged to make more British TV to head off a Labour challenge to the Paramount-Warner Bros merger.

Mr Ellison, who leads Paramount, has vowed to boost investment in original UK shows on Channel 5 after Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, threatened to intervene in the $110bn (£83bn) deal because of its effect on media plurality.

As part of legally binding commitments to win approval, Paramount, which owns Channel 5, said new commissions on the channel would “prioritise UK-originated content, including original drama, factual and entertainment programming”.

It has also promised to ensure Channel 5 News maintains its “editorial independence” and to broadcast at least 600 hours of kids TV per year through its Milkshake! shows.

The move meant the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) as well as the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), the competition watchdog, were able to approve the merger.

The Hollywood tie-up is poised to combine Paramount, which also owns CBS News as well as Nickelodeon and Comedy Central, with Warner’s slate of properties including CNN, TNT Sports and Cartoon Network.

The deal will also affect 4,000 Warner Bros staff in the UK. The Hollywood giant has made several major movies in its Leavesden studios in Hertfordshire in recent years, including Barbie and Wonka.

The CMA cleared the deal after investigating concerns about the impact of reducing the number of major Hollywood studios from five to four.

A CMA spokesman said it had cleared the blockbuster merger “as it does not raise competition concerns in the UK”.

They added that its investigation found that following the deal, Paramount “will continue to face sufficient competition” across TV and film production as well as streaming services.

Separately, Ms Nandy had written to Paramount and Warner Bros just weeks ago saying she was “minded to intervene” in the merger between the two Hollywood giants.

Ms Nandy’s decision not to intervene in the merger between the two Hollywood film studios means that Ofcom, the regulator, will not conduct a formal public interest investigation into the deal.

The Culture Secretary will also meet the Hollywood giant in the coming weeks to secure pledges about the impact of the mega-merger deal on Britain’s wider creative industry.

A statement from the department said that the set of guarantees from Paramount will “help safeguard the continued availability of a diverse range of broadcasting and on-demand services in the UK”.

It marks a boost for the merger which has become bogged down in recent months by a legal challenge from 12 American states.

The US department of justice has already cleared the deal, although it still faces state opposition and clearance from the American communications regulator.

Mr Ellison, a supporter of Donald Trump and the son of the tech billionaire Larry Ellison, has also received pushback on the deal from staff at CNN and Hollywood stars such as Jane Fonda and Ben Stiller.

Paramount has said it expects the deal to be completed by the end of September. However, there are fears that the legal challenge will hold up the merger.

A month-long delay could become very costly for Paramount. The company previously pledged to start paying Warner Bros’ shareholders an added ticking-fee compensation amounting to about $7m (£5.2m) per day if the deal wasn’t closed by Sept 30.

Paramount said it was “pleased to have agreed on a path forward” with the DCMS. It added that the decision by the CMA “directly refutes the assumptions” made in the legal complaint led by the state of California.

Warner Bros was contacted for comment.
